Primo capolavoro di prosa narrativa che folgora e conquista la societa dell'Europa moderna, Il Decameron narra le cento novelle che sette gentili fanciulle e tre cortesi giovani, rufugiati sulle colline fiesolane per evitare il contagio della terribile peste che nel 1348 infierisce su Firenze, si raccontano lungo il corso di dieci giornate. Piu di cinquecento opere d'arte dei secoli X...
commentaries: Northrop Frye states that collections like the Decameron, using a symposium device, belong to the contemplative, 'penseroso' phase of romance.
Northrop Frye cites Boccaccio's Decameron as an example of a work of fiction composed of short stories, analogous to the structure of a confession.
Erich Auerbach directly cites Boccaccio's 'The Decameron' as the primary source text being analyzed, providing the original Italian and an English translation.
Michel de Montaigne lists the Decameron as a book worth reading for amusement among modern pleasant works.
Harold Bloom identifies Boccaccio's Decameron as the likely model for Chaucer's Canterbury Tales, despite Chaucer never explicitly mentioning it.
Erich Auerbach introduces a novella from Boccaccio's Decameron as an example to analyze, summarizing its plot.
Erich Auerbach uses Boccaccio's Decameron as a chronological reference point, noting that the text under discussion is over a century more recent.
Erich Auerbach contrasts the Franco-Burgundian stories with Boccaccio's work, listing specific stylistic and thematic elements absent from the imitations.

book:23504468.description: The war is over and the hero returns. But what good is a hero without a war? What else does he know but warfare? And his city has managed without him. The gap left by his departure has closed. Yet the problems he left behind have remained. They have lain dormant. But his return revives them.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne cites Seneca to support his view that uncertain misfortunes are more tormenting than definite ones.
Michel de Montaigne quotes a proverb found in Rabelais' work 'Gargantua' to support the critique of pedants.
Umberto Eco uses Rabelais’s Gargantua as a prime example of rhythmic hypotyposis, where verbal cadence creates a vivid visual effect beyond mere listing.

book:web_78839363.description: A work of natural theology attempting to demonstrate religious truths through observation of the natural world without reliance on scripture or revelation. Also known as 'The Book of Creatures.'
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne describes his father receiving this book from Peter Bunel, noting it was considered useful during the rise of Lutheran doctrines.

book:551602.description: This is the first volume of an anthology of Latin poetry. The two-volume anthology covers a period of four and a half centuries, beginning with the work of the mime-writer Publilius Syrus, who flourished ca. 45 BCE, and ending with the graphic and charming poem of Rutilius Namatianus recording a sea voyage from Rome to Gaul in 416 CE. A wide variety of theme gives interest to the poems: hunting in a poem of Grattius; an inquiry into the causes of volcanic activity by the author of "Aetna"; pastoral poems by...
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne quotes Calpurnius's Eclogues to illustrate the opulent, jeweled decorations of the Roman amphitheatres, emphasizing their extravagant material splendor.
Michel de Montaigne quotes Calpurnius's Eclogues to vividly depict the engineered spectacles and marvels of the Roman games, highlighting their mechanical ingenuity and fantastical displays.
Michel de Montaigne cites Calpurnius again (from the same work, Eclogues) to emphasize the extreme luxury of the protective nets in the arena, which were woven with gold threads.

book:web_a06478c1.description: Julius Caesar's firsthand account of the Gallic Wars, written as a series of commentaries. It details his military campaigns in Gaul from 58 to 50 BC. The work was widely circulated in manuscript form in antiquity and was a standard text in Renaissance education.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne notes that Caesar elaborates on his engineering feats in his work 'De Bello Gallico', while being brief on his military valor.

book:web_1726a5da.description: A speech of praise delivered by Pliny the Younger to Emperor Trajan in 100 AD, later published as a model of panegyric oratory. It celebrates Trajan's virtues and contrasts him favorably with previous emperors like Domitian.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Pliny's 'Panegyric' as a factual source on Trajan's education and talents.
Edward Gibbon mentions Pliny's Panegyric as a source on the mildness and precision of tax laws under Trajan and the Antonines.

book:web_13f33ed4.description: A collection of short chapters on grammar, philosophy, history, antiquarianism, and other subjects, preserving fragments of many authors and works that otherwise would have been lost. The title translates to 'Attic Nights', referring to long winter nights spent in Attica.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne cites Aulus Gellius's 'Attic Nights' to argue that excessive reliance on subordinates' judgment undermines authority.
Jorge Luis Borges cites Aulus Gellius's work as containing a version of a paradoxical syllogism, similar to others mentioned.
Jorge Luis Borges cites Aulus Gellius's 'Attic Nights' as a source for the story of Archytas's flying dove, connecting it to Wilkins's predictions about lunar travel.

Umberto Eco cites Aulus Gellius’s ancient text as a concrete example of historical challenges in interpreting color terminology, highlighting the limits of linguistic and perceptual reconstruction across time.
Edward Gibbon cites Aulus Gellius's Attic Nights to support a point about the status of municipal cities and colonies during the reign of Hadrian.

book:3227621.description: "Sources and Backgrounds" includes Seneca's inspired commentary on Ovid, Charles Martin's essay on the ways in which pantomimic dancing--an art form popular in Ovid's time--may have been the model forMetamorphoses, as well as related works by Virgil, Callimachus, Hesiod, and Lucretius, among others. From the enormous body of scholarly writing onMetamorphoses, Charles Martin has chosen six major interpretations by Bernard Knox, J. R. R. Mackail, Norman O. Brown, Italo Calvino, Frederick Ahl, and Diane Middle...
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne quotes Ovid's 'Metamorphoses' to use the myth of Niobe as an allegory for the stupefying effect of overwhelming grief, linking it to the theme of sorrow's physical manifestations.
Michel de Montaigne recalls that his earliest enjoyment of books came from reading Ovid's Metamorphoses in childhood, finding it the easiest and most age-appropriate text available to him.
Michel de Montaigne quotes Ovid's Metamorphoses to convey a willingness to entrust future events to fortune.
Joseph Campbell references Ovid's 'Metamorphoses' as a source of myths that illustrate the dangerous transformations resulting from the sudden removal of insulation from a power center.
Joseph Campbell references Ovid's 'Metamorphoses' as a source of mythological examples of gods disguising themselves to approach nymphs.
Joseph Campbell cites a specific passage from Ovid's work, noting the translator and edition.
Joseph Campbell cites specific passages from Ovid's epic poem as a reference.
Joseph Campbell references Ovid's 'Metamorphoses' as a source for the classical myth of Hermaphrodites.
Joseph Campbell cites specific passages from Ovid's 'Metamorphoses' for additional examples related to the narrative.
Joseph Campbell cites a specific passage from Ovid's work as a reference.
Joseph Campbell cites specific passages from Ovid's work.
Joseph Campbell cites specific lines from Ovid's epic poem.
Michel de Montaigne quotes Ovid to describe a scene of extreme cold where wine froze solid and was distributed in pieces.
Michel de Montaigne cites Ovid's 'Tristia' to illustrate the paradoxical pleasure found in weeping.
Michel de Montaigne quotes Ovid's Tristia to describe his own natural inclination towards avoiding troubles and seeking a quiet life.

book:20385662.description: The Ars amatoria (English: The Art of Love) is an instructional book series elegy in three books by Ancient Rome Roman poet Ovid. It was written in 2 AD. It is about teaching basic Gentlemanly male and female relationship skills and techniques. Ovid offers advice to men on subjects such as, how to seduce and keep a woman, and also notably offers women advice on how to be attractive to men. He advises that, "if one is accompanying a lady to the horse-racing in the Circus Maximus, one should gallantly brush t...
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne quotes Ovid's Ars Amatoria to vividly describe the physical distortions of anger, illustrating why it impairs judgment.
Michel de Montaigne quotes Ovid's 'Ars Amatoria' (The Art of Love) to argue against jealousy, suggesting love is not diminished by being shared.
Umberto Eco cites Ovid's The Art of Love to illustrate ancient resistance to traditional forms and the early assertion of modernity in literature.

book:20738843.description:
This is an alternate cover edition for ISBN13: 9780140423556
In the twenty-one poems of the "Heroides", Ovid gave voice to the heroines and heroes of epic and myth. These deeply moving literary epistles reveal the happiness and torment of love, as the writers tell of their pain at separation, forgiveness of infidelity or anger at betrayal. The faithful Penelope wonders at the suspiciously long absence of Ulysses, while Dido bitterly reproaches Aeneas for too eagerly leaving her bed to follow his destiny, an...
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne quotes Ovid to express personal experience where cunning or worldly wisdom failed, while straightforwardness succeeded.

book:3077838.description: Ovid's "Amores" translated by Guy Lee in the 1960s.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne references Ovid's 'Amores' to humorously underscore the extent and endurance of his youthful sexual vigor.
Michel de Montaigne cites Ovid's work to support the idea that imagination can transmit harm, similar to physical contagion.
Edward Gibbon references Ovid's 'Fasti' as a source on Roman festivals, noting it is an incomplete work covering only the first six months of the year.

book:web_fba5fb01.description: A seminal work on Roman military organization, tactics, and equipment by the classical scholar Justus Lipsius. It was highly influential in early modern military thought and antiquarian studies of ancient Rome.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon directs the reader to Lipsius's work for detailed information on Roman legionary arms.

book:web_2fa81959.description: A treatise on the greatness of ancient Rome, focusing on its population, military strength, and urban dimensions. Part of Lipsius's antiquarian scholarship on Roman civilization.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon again cites Lipsius's work, this time for information on the Roman navy.
Edward Gibbon directs the reader to Lipsius's work for further information on the size and organization of the Roman military.
Edward Gibbon cites Lipsius's book 'de magnitudine Romana' for numerical details about the Praetorian Guard.
Edward Gibbon references Lipsius's work as providing a scholarly defense of a textual interpretation related to Constantine's birth.

book:web_eb4ca4bb.description: A treatise by the renowned humanist Justus Lipsius on the pronunciation of the Latin language, arguing for a reconstructed classical pronunciation over the medieval ecclesiastical one.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Lipsius's specific work on Latin pronunciation by chapter in a footnote.

book:web_82842cb9.description: A scholarly treatise on Roman assemblies and political institutions by the French humanist Nicolas de Grouchy (c. 1510–1572). The work analyzes the comitia (popular assemblies) of ancient Rome and was influential in Renaissance political thought.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne mentions Nicolas Grouchy as one of his domestic tutors and notes his authorship of a book on Roman assemblies.

book:144513.description: ..". gives us all sixteen of the satires in the tough, slashing manner of the original, unheard in Dryden and the few others who tried it." --Saturday Review
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne cites Juvenal to support the philosophical argument that glory, in and of itself, is worthless.
Michel de Montaigne quotes Juvenal's Satires to illustrate the commonness of valiant deaths and their lack of lasting renown.
Michel de Montaigne quotes Juvenal's 'Satires' to vividly describe the furious rage of parents beating their children, emphasizing the intensity of their anger.
Michel de Montaigne quotes Juvenal's Satires to argue that a citizen's value lies in their utility to the state, framing the discussion on child-rearing.
Michel de Montaigne quotes Juvenal to satirize the learned who excessively parade their knowledge in all discourse, even in intimate matters.

book:11381743.description: The date of composition of the Metamorphoses is uncertain. It's variously been considered by scholars as a youthful work preceding Apuleius' Apology of 158/9, or as the climax of his literary career & perhaps as late as the 170s or 180s. Apuleius adapted the story from a Greek original of which the author's name is said to be Lucius of Patrae (the name of the lead character & narrator). This Greek text has been lost, but there is Loukios e onos (Loukios e onos, Loukios/Lucius or the Ass), a similar tale of....
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges cites 'The Golden Ass' as an example of the nomadic, random genre of adventure narratives, alongside other works like 'Don Quixote'.
Jorge Luis Borges mentions 'The Golden Ass' as an example of a work with a sequential, less rigid plot structure.
The excerpt lists a book by Apuleio in a bibliographic format, but it is presented as a reference within the narrative context, likely as a source for ideas discussed.
Joseph Campbell cites Apuleius's work, though the specific reference is cut off in the excerpt.
Umberto Eco references Apuleius’s The Golden Ass as one of the few classical literary sources depicting witches, using it to contrast ancient perceptions of witchcraft with later modern demonization.
Edward Gibbon references Apuleius's work as a humorous description of the priests of the Syrian goddess.

book:13809066.description:
A classic of the ancient world of warfare
De Re Militari (Concerning Military Affairs), written in the 5th century by Vegetius and translated from the original Latin, is a treatise on warfare in the Roman world and is vital reading for any modern student of the subject as it clearly outlines the methods and practices of the type of warfare waged by the Roman Empire at the height of its power. So influential was Vegetius' book that it was considered as an essential field-guide well into the age of gunpowder....
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Vegetius's work on military matters as a source for information on the Roman legion.
Edward Gibbon cites Vegetius's work on military matters, noting it as an abridgment of regulations from the time of Trajan and Hadrian.
Edward Gibbon references Vegetius's work for a linguistic point about the term 'miles' in different historical periods.
Edward Gibbon cites Vegetius's work on military science to provide evidence about the cavalry composition of the Imperial legion.

book:1209722.description: The Adelphoe (The Brothers) of Terence is a Latin adaptation of a comedy of the same name by the Greek comic playwright Menander. The theme of the play is the perennially interesting question of the relationship between the generations and the proper way to bring up a son. In the introduction Mr Martin considers Terence in the context of Roman comedy generally and discusses the background of the Adelphoe. There is also a section on metre and scansion and a short analysis of the textual tradition. The full a...
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne cites Terence's Adelphoe to express despair over the irredeemable state of society.

book:1062328.description:
Terence brought to the Roman stage a bright comic voice and a refined sense of style. His six comedies - first produced in the half dozen years before his premature death in 159 B.C. - imaginatively reformulated in Latin plays written by Greek playwrights, especially Menander.
For this new Loeb Classical Library edition of Terence, John Barsby gives us a faithful and lively translation with full explanatory notes, facing a freshly edited Latin text.
Volume I contains a substantial introduction and three pla...
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne quotes Terence's Heauton Timorumenos to articulate his self-imposed abstinence from pleasure in the absence of his friend, underscoring their shared existence.
Michel de Montaigne quotes a line from Terence's play 'Heauton Timorumenos' to illustrate a point about personal appearance and interpretation.

book:web_17151790.description: A Latin comedy by Terence (Publius Terentius Afer), also known as 'The Brothers'. It contrasts two approaches to parenting through the characters of strict Demea and indulgent Micio.
commentaries: Northrop Frye uses Terence's play 'Adelphoi' as an example to illustrate the contrast between humorous bondage and pragmatic freedom in comedy.

Michel de Montaigne quotes Martial's epigram to recount the story of Arria and Paetus, using it to highlight the nobility and courage of Arria's action, though he notes that the poet's expression falls short of the action's true bravery.
Umberto Eco cites Martial's Epigrams as a classical example of hostile female portrayal in literature, using it to illustrate the long-standing tradition of demonizing women in satire.
Edward Gibbon lists Martial as one of the notable literary figures produced by Spain.
Edward Gibbon references Martial as another poet who provided firsthand descriptions of the amphitheatre, comparing his approach to that of Calphurnius.
Joseph Campbell quotes a line from Martial's 'Epigrams' to illustrate a point about dual inheritance or nature.

book:web_2fd9b58b.description: A Latin poem in elegiac couplets describing the author's sea voyage from Rome to Gaul in 416 CE. The work is often cited as 'Itinerarium' or 'De Reditu Suo' and contains the quoted line about the plague spreading when lanced.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne cites Rutilius to present a view that punishment may spread vice rather than curb it.
Harold Bloom quotes from Hazlitt's book 'Characters of Shakespeare’s Plays' to illustrate the relationship between poetry, rhetoric, and political power.

book:38154.description: The only unabridged prose translation of Ariosto's Orlando Furioso- a witty parody of the chivalric legends of Charlemagne and the Saracen invasion of France - this version faithfully recaptures the entire narrative and the subtle meanings behind it.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne quotes Ariosto's epic poem to illustrate the idea that true virtue lies in performing brave actions for their own sake, not for the sake of being witnessed or narrated.
Northrop Frye cites Orlando Furioso as an example of a Renaissance narrative where the primary interest is storytelling, though it can be interpreted thematically.
Harold Bloom identifies Ariosto's 'Orlando Furioso' as the great prototype for Don Quixote's madness, specifically citing the character Orlando's erotic madness.

book:web_4d944d78.description: A compilation of biographies and sayings of ancient Greek philosophers, written in Greek in the 3rd century AD. The work includes a 'Life of Arcesilaus' (often spelled Archesilaus), the skeptical philosopher who headed the Platonic Academy.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne quotes a witty saying of Arcesilaus as recorded by Diogenes Laertius in his 'Life of Archesilaus', using it to comment on philosophical schools.

book:web_041329cf.description: Third book of Ficino's 'De vita libri tres' (Three Books on Life), focusing on astral magic and how to draw down celestial influences. It was the most popular and widely read of his works during the Renaissance.
commentaries: Frances A. Yates states that Ficino outlines his magic in the book 'De vita coelitus comparanda', describing it as his most popular and widely read work.

book:486013.description: A Critical Edition and Translation with Introduction and Notes
commentaries: The excerpt states that Ficino was aware of the pseudo-Aristotelian theory and mentioned it in his work De triplici vita.

book:web_4ae70c45.description: Collection of elegiac letters written by Ovid during his exile to Tomis on the Black Sea, addressed to various friends and supporters in Rome, pleading for his recall.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne quotes Ovid's verse from 'De Ponto' to express his own dissatisfaction with his writings, using it as a comparison to illustrate his self-criticism.
Michel de Montaigne quotes Ovid's 'De Ponto' to emphasize that no authority can justify betraying a friend, even for public service.
Michel de Montaigne references Ovid's 'De Pont' to illustrate the Roman custom of kissing in greeting.

book:web_4e9add55.description: Ovid's 'Fasti' is a six-book Latin poem on the Roman calendar, detailing religious festivals, astronomical events, and historical anniversaries. The work was composed around 8 CE and left unfinished due to Ovid's exile.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Ovid's work to provide a description of the festival of the Megalesia, noting its duration and the public celebrations.

book:13583390.description:
Author: Desiderius Erasmus
Illustrator: Franz Masereel
Format/binding: Hardcover
Binding: Hardcover
Publisher: Joh, Enshede En Zonen
Place: Haarlem, Holland
Date published: 1943
From http://www.ourcivilisation.com/smartb...
The bantering tone, the attack on the theologians and the satire on widely practised religious observances provoked a reaction of shocked hostility during Erasmus's lifetime. Erasmus regarded the Praise of Folly as a minor work and, in his letter to Dorp (p. t38), said that he almost reg...
commentaries: Frances A. Yates identifies this as the famous work by Erasmus, drawing a direct comparison to Agrippa's 'De vanitate'.
The excerpt references a work by Erasmo (Erasmus) in a bibliographic entry, indicating it as a source for the discussion on folly or related themes.
Northrop Frye references Erasmus's book as part of the encyclopaedic satire tradition, illustrating its connection to comic phases.

book:4225755.description: This is one of seven volumes that will contain the more than 4000 adages that Erasmus gathered and commented on, sometimes in a few lines and sometimes in full-scale essays. The notes identify the classical sources and indicate how Erasmus' reading and thinking developed over the quarter-century spanned by the eight revisions of the original work. Many of the proverbs cited by Erasmus are still in our common stock of speech.
commentaries: Erich Auerbach suggests Erasmus's Adagia as a possible direct source for Rabelais's use of the Silenus comparison.

book:web_5b36bd59.description: A panegyric poem by Claudian celebrating the sixth consulship of the Roman Emperor Honorius in 404 AD. It is a major work of Late Latin literature.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne cites a Latin verse from Claudius to support the argument that true victory lies in subduing the enemy's spirit.

book:web_cd3a8aca.description: One of the books of the Hebrew Bible/Old Testament, traditionally attributed to King Solomon. It is a philosophical reflection on the meaning of life, famously declaring 'Vanity of vanities; all is vanity.'
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne references the Book of Ecclesiastes to underscore the theme of vanity, which he is meditating upon in his essay.

book:web_ed66ea85.description: A lost work by Antisthenes, founder of Cynic philosophy, referenced in ancient sources but not extant. Likely discussed themes of education, mentorship, and relationships between teacher and student.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne mentions two books by Antisthenes, with alternative titles, questioning their subjects in a list of works on love and procreation.

book:web_e9e32c11.description: A lost work by Antisthenes, the founder of Cynic philosophy, referenced by ancient authors. The title suggests it was a philosophical treatise on marriage and procreation.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne mentions two books by Antisthenes, with alternative titles, questioning their subjects in a list of works on love and procreation.

book:web_a73db2bc.description: A methodological work on how to study and understand history, written by the French jurist and political philosopher Jean Bodin. It presents a systematic approach to historical study and is considered an important early work in historiography.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne mentions Jean Bodin's work 'Methodus ad facilem historiarum cognitionem' as having sufficiently addressed the obscurity of self-knowledge in historical matters.

book:web_cf2e8eba.description: A major treatise on witchcraft and demonology by the French jurist and political philosopher Jean Bodin, arguing for the reality of witchcraft and advocating harsh prosecution of witches.
commentaries: Frances A. Yates states that King James I refers the reader to Bodin's work for examples of witchcraft.
Frances A. Yates references the publication date of Bodin's 'Démonomanie' as a historical marker.
Frances A. Yates cites Bodin's book as a devastating attack on the use of Kabbalah by Pico della Mirandola and Agrippa.
Frances A. Yates cites Bodin's work to reference his arguments against magic and the Kabbalah.

book:web_80662323.description: A lost work on love by the Stoic philosopher Cleanthes, mentioned in ancient sources such as Diogenes Laërtius' 'Lives of the Philosophers' (3rd century CE).
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne mentions two books by Cleanthes, questioning their content in a list of philosophical works on love.

book:web_b43f8fe8.description: A geographical work by the Roman historian Arrian, describing a voyage around the Black Sea (Euxine Sea). It was written as a report to Emperor Hadrian around 131-132 AD, detailing coastal landmarks, distances, and Roman military installations.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Arrian's 'Periplus of the Euxine' for details on military garrisons and geography.

book:web_2a3a829e.description: A philosophical dialogue on love, attributed to Demetrius of Phalerum (c. 350–280 BCE), an Athenian orator and Peripatetic philosopher. The work is known from ancient references but is now lost.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne mentions a specific book by Demetrius Phalereus, questioning its content in a list of works on love.

book:505222.description: In the early 1500s five men and five women find themselves trapped by floods and compelled to take refuge in an abbey high in the Pyrenees. When told they must wait days for a bridge to be repaired, they are inspired - by recalling Boccaccio's Decameron - to pass the time in a cultured manner by each telling a story every day. The stories, however, soon degenerate into a verbal battle between the sexes, as the characters weave tales of corrupt friars, adulterous noblemen and deceitful wives. From the cynica...
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne references a specific tale in the 'Heptameron' by the Queen of Navarre, disagreeing with its portrayal of a chaste encounter as miraculous, while also offering a brief positive comment on the book itself.

book:web_bc0ebfd0.description: A collection of biographies of famous men, including a biography of Titus Pomponius Atticus. The 'Life of Atticus' is one of the surviving sections of this work.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne concludes with a quote from Cornelius Nepos to assert that individual character, rather than external power, shapes one's fortune.

book:15953862.description: Drawn from James B. Atkinson and David Sices' Montaigne: Selected Essays, this annotated translation of Etienne de La Boetie's political masterpiece offers an ideal opportunity to become acquainted with the thought of a brilliant though short-lived sixteenth-century French thinker known for "his mortal and sworn hatred for all vice," as his friend Michel de Montaigne put it, "but particularly for that sordid traffic concocted under the honorable title of justice." Atkinson's Introduction fleshes out a portr...
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne borrows this discourse by Estienne de la Boetie to adorn his own work, praising it as finely written and full, though noting it was written in youth and falls short of what Boetie might have achieved later.
Michel de Montaigne suggests that a brief comment in Plutarch may have inspired La Boetie's book 'Voluntary Servitude'.

book:web_aa1e3fbc.description: A collection of pastoral poems falsely attributed to the Roman poet Gallus (Gaius Cornelius Gallus, c. 70–26 BCE) in the Renaissance. The actual author is unknown, but the poems circulated under this pseudonym in the 16th century and were included in early printed editions of Virgil's works.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne quotes a passage from Pseudo-Gallus's 'Eclogues' to illustrate the oppressive nature of life under strict regimens, using it to argue against depriving oneself of accustomed pleasures.

book:527507.description: In The Book of the Courtier (1528), Baldesar Castiglione, a diplomat and Papal Nuncio to Rome, sets out to define the essential virtues for those at Court. In a lively series of imaginary conversations between the real-life courtiers to the Duke of Urbino, his speakers discuss qualities of noble behaviour - chiefly discretion, decorum, nonchalance and gracefulness - as well as wider questions such as the duties of a good government and the true nature of love. Castiglione's narrative power and psychological...
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne cites Castiglione's 'The Courtier' for its opinion on the social disgrace of riding a mule.
Northrop Frye references Castiglione as the source of the concept of the 'graceful courtier,' which contributes to the thematic meaning of 'grace' in Renaissance comedy.
Erich Auerbach cites Castiglione's book 'Il Cortegiano' as the most famous illustration of the later fusion of Platonism and the courtly ideal.

book:15777533.description:
Ideale rappresentante dell'autunno del Rinascimento, la Gerusalemme liberatadivenne ben presto uno tra i libri piu letti e amati in tutta Europa.
Tasso seppe descrivere con il suo poema un mondo umano e narrativo chiaroscurale, ricco di una tensione mai completamente risolta tra etica e desiderio, tra doveri nei confronti di una giustizia superiore e umanissimi cedimenti alle debolezze. Nel contrasto allargato alle grandi forze del Cielo e dell'Inferno, la Liberatacomunica un profondo senso di crisi attrave...
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges uses Tasso's epic poem as an example of a work from which allegorical meanings can be derived.
Jorge Luis Borges discusses Tasso's 'Gerusalemme liberate' as a notable epic poem, contrasting it with its less successful revision.
Jorge Luis Borges references Tasso's epic poem as the third and least successful variation of a motif originating in Homer.
Northrop Frye lists Jerusalem Delivered as an example of a national epic from the high mimetic period, unified by patriotic and religious ideas.

book:web_e6634e53.description: A revised version of Tasso's epic poem 'Gerusalemme Liberata' (Jerusalem Delivered), written to conform more strictly to Counter-Reformation religious orthodoxy and Aristotelian literary principles. It is generally considered artistically inferior to the original.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges references Tasso's 'Conquistata' as a revised version of his epic that failed to achieve literary significance.
Jorge Luis Borges mentions Tasso alongside Milton and Virgil as poets committed to their craft.

book:9076267.description:
Testo latino a fronte.
A military leader of legendary genius, Caesar was also a great writer, recording the events of his life with incomparable immediacy and power The Civil Waris a tense and gripping depiction of his struggle with Pompey over the leadership of Republican Rome - a conflict that spanned the entire Roman world, from Gaul and Spain to Asia and Africa. Where Caesar's own account leaves off in 48 BC, his lieutenants take up the history, describing the vital battles of Munda, Spain and Thapsus,....
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne cites Caesar's 'De Bello Civili' to illustrate that the Roman practice of fighting with rapier and cloak was similar to a contemporary custom.

book:web_54695c27.description: Julius Caesar's firsthand account of the Gallic Wars, written as a series of commentaries. The work was composed during the war (c. 58–50 BCE) and circulated in Rome. The abbreviation 'de Bell. Gallic.' is a standard Latin reference to this classic historical and military text.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Caesar's commentary on the Gallic Wars as a primary historical source regarding the geography and limits of ancient Germany.
Edward Gibbon cites Caesar's 'De Bello Gallico' as a source for information about the Germans.
Edward Gibbon cites a specific book (VI) and chapter (23) of Caesar's 'de Bello Gallico' (The Gallic War) as a footnote reference for information on German warfare and territorial practices.

book:web_1a35453b.description: Julius Caesar's firsthand account of the Roman Civil War against Pompey and the Senate, covering events from 49-48 BCE. Written as a continuation of his Commentarii de Bello Gallico.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Caesar's own 'Commentaries' on the Civil War as a source for his actions in defense of tribunitian rights.

book:551328.description: In this volume are three works concerning the campaigns engaged in by the great Roman statesman Julius Caesar (10044 BCE), but not written by him. "The Alexandrian War, " which deals with troubles elsewhere also, may have been written by Aulus Hirtius (ca. 9043 BC, friend and military subordinate of Caesar), who is generally regarded as the author of the last book of Caesar's "Gallic War.""The African War" and "The Spanish War" are detailed accounts clearly by officers who had shared in the campaigns. All t...
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Hirtius's work 'de Bello Alexandrino' for a description of Alexandria.

book:web_c4ca58bb.description: A fictionalized biography of Aesop, written in the Hellenistic period, blending legend and folklore about the legendary fabulist. It survives in later Byzantine recensions and is not attributable to a single known author.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites this Hellenic text to illustrate how physical ugliness was attributed to Aesop, contrasting his moral and intellectual value with his appearance.

book:web_2e915c7f.description: A foundational Christian apologetic work by Lactantius, written in the early 4th century, which systematically defends Christianity against pagan beliefs and philosophies.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Lactantius's work as an example of early Christian rejection of the spherical Earth, using biblical literalism to argue for a rectangular cosmos.
Edward Gibbon cites Lactantius as a source of evidence regarding the choice of Constantine by his dying father.
Edward Gibbon directs the reader to Lactantius for details on the financial inquisition and use of torture under Galerius.
Edward Gibbon cites Lactantius as a partial and injudicious source for an anecdote about a private conversation between Diocletian and Galerius, questioning its truth and decency.
Edward Gibbon quotes Lactantius to describe the rapid and improbable promotion of Maximin from humble origins to the rank of Caesar.
Edward Gibbon acknowledges Lactantius as a source that even praises the diligence and fidelity of the emperor Severus.
Edward Gibbon attributes a report about Galerius's long-term imperial schemes to Lactantius, while casting strong doubt on its reliability.

book:web_c7a2cf45.description: A theological work by Lactantius, also known as 'Divine Institutes', written in the early 4th century AD. It is an apologetic work defending Christianity against pagan critics and explaining Christian doctrine.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Lactantius's 'Divine Institutes' as a source describing prophecies of future calamities with eloquence.

book:web_ce36d4e5.description: A collection of neo-Latin love poems (kisses) by the Dutch poet Johannes Secundus, first published posthumously in 1539. The work was highly influential in Renaissance poetry and inspired many imitations.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne cites the Basia as a pleasant modern work, though he questions if it fits the title of 'book'.

book:web_f120e8a2.description: A collection of moralizing letters by Spanish bishop and chronicler Antonio de Guevara, commonly known in English as 'Golden Epistles' or 'Familiar Epistles'. The work was widely popular across Europe in the 16th century.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne mentions obtaining information from Guevara's 'Letters' (referred to as 'Golden Epistles') but expresses a low personal opinion of the work.

book:17818767.description: Aeschylus was the first of the three ancient Greek tragedians whose plays can still be read or performed, the others being Sophocles and Euripides. He is often described as the father of tragedy: our knowledge of the genre begins with his work and our understanding of earlier tragedies is largely based on inferences from his surviving plays. Only seven of his estimated seventy to ninety plays have survived into modern times. Fragments of some other plays have survived in quotes and more continue to be disco...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Aeschylus’s Agamemnon as a prime example of ancient textual density, using it to illustrate how translation must reconstruct the emotional and stylistic rhythm of original works.

book:237794.description:
Essa peca e considerada unica entre as tragedias remanescentes do periodo por retratar um evento historico - a guerra entre os gregos e os persas - em vez de dramatizar uma epoca distante, de herois miticos. A peca gira em torno do desastre em que os invasores da Grecia viram suas forcas navais aniquiladas pelos gregos na Batalha de Salamina.
A acao se passa na capital persa onde um mensageiro leva a rainha a noticia do desastre. Depois de atribuir a derrota da Persia a independencia e bravura gregas assim....
commentaries: Northrop Frye cites Aeschylus's play 'The Persians' as an example of a tragedy associated with a historical occasion of national rejoicing, to argue against tragedy producing real sorrow.

book:475080.description: A shrine is stronger than a tower to save, A shield that none may cleave. Step swift thereto, And in your left hands hold with reverence The white-crowned wands of suppliance, the sign Beloved of Zeus, compassion's lord, and speak To those that question you, words meek and low And piteous, as beseems your stranger state,
commentaries: Northrop Frye references Aeschylus's play 'The Suppliants' as an example to illustrate the musical structure underlying early drama.

book:web_02f930ae.description: A collection of historical anecdotes and sayings in nine books, compiled during the reign of Tiberius (14–37 AD). Commonly known as 'Memorable Deeds and Sayings' or simply 'Valerius Maximus'.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne references Valerius Maximus as a source for an anecdote about a death caused by a grape-stone, exemplifying death's trivial causes.
Michel de Montaigne cites Valerius Maximus for an extreme example of thirst during a siege in Crete.
Michel de Montaigne references Valerius Maximus's 'Factorum ac Dictorum Memorabilium Libri IX' to argue that compelled actions credit the enforcer rather than the performer.
Michel de Montaigne references Valerius Maximus to critique the decline of military discipline.

book:web_7788b9a5.description: Collection of Latin poems by Scottish humanist, scholar and poet George Buchanan, first published in 1584. The work includes various poetic forms and celebrates Scottish themes.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Buchanan's 'Sylvae' as a poetic celebration of Scottish independence.

book:web_3953b152.description: A concise history of Rome from its founding to the reign of Emperor Valens, written in Latin by the historian Eutropius in the 4th century AD. It was widely used as a school text in antiquity and the Middle Ages.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Eutropius's work to provide historical details about the character and policies of the emperor Constantius.

book:web_dbe4d2bf.description: A geographical and political description of Greece by the ancient Greek philosopher and geographer Dicaearchus of Messana (c. 350–285 BCE). The work survives only in fragments, notably compiled in 'Geographi Graeci Minores' edited by Karl Müller (1855) and earlier in 'Geographiae Veteris Scriptores Graeci Minores' edited by John Hudson (1698–1712).
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Dicaearchus's work to support an observation about the modest simplicity of private houses in ancient Athens.

book:web_b6c71cf3.description: A historical study of Russian foreign policy and influence in the Balkan region, published by Oxford University Press.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt lists two books by B. H. Sumner as part of a bibliography or reference list.
Hannah Arendt cites this book to reference Dulles's explanation of the CIA's role.
Hannah Arendt cites Allan W. Dulles's statement to support the claim about the influential position of intelligence services in the U.S. government.

book:web_35c0f407.description: A legal and administrative work by Hans Frank, a prominent Nazi jurist and Governor-General of occupied Poland, published in Munich in 1939.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt references Frank's book to illustrate the ideological presentation of the Nazi regime as based on loyalty rather than dictatorship.

book:web_86a28b6d.description: A historical study of the Pan-German League (Alldeutscher Verband), a German nationalist organization active from 1890 to 1918, published as part of the 'Historische Studien' monograph series.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt references Werner's book as a source of useful information on the Pan-German League.

book:web_fd2f37d9.description: A history of Bolshevism from its origins to the early 1930s, written by the German Marxist historian Arthur Rosenberg. Originally published in German in 1932 as 'Geschichte des Bolschewismus'.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt cites Rosenberg's book for a detailed description of how party members destroyed the Soviet system from within.
Hannah Arendt references Rosenberg's book to illustrate the dual structure of power in Soviet Russia, contrasting the formal Soviet government with the actual rule of the Bolshevik Party.

book:web_409619b9.description: A 10-volume universal cultural history of humanity by German ethnographer and librarian Gustav Friedrich Klemm, published between 1843 and 1852. It was an influential early work in the field of cultural anthropology and ethnology.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt references Klemm's cultural history, possibly as an early work in anthropology.

book:691614.description:
Originally published 1937; this is a reprint of the second edition of 1948.
Nikolai Berdyaev (1874-1948), born into the Russian aristocratic intelligentsia, was, as a young Marxist, sentenced in 1897 to three years of internal exile for illegal political activity.
After turning from Marxism toward Christianity, his 1913 criticism of the Orthodox Church led him to be charged with blasphemy, a crime for which he would have been liable to permanent Siberian exile, though WWI and the 1917 Revolution prevented h...
commentaries: Hannah Arendt references Berdyaev's book for a specific page on Russian communism.
Hannah Arendt cites Berdyaev's book, likely to reference an analysis of Russian communism.

book:web_2f324756.description: A study of Soviet foreign policy and internal politics by the Russian-born American historian and political writer David J. Dallin, analyzing the transition from Stalinist purges to post-Stalin international relations.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt lists this book as part of a bibliography or reference list.
Hannah Arendt references Dallin's work on Soviet concentration camps, noting its sometimes less convincing nature due to sources from prominent personalities.
Hannah Arendt references Dallin's book to critique the economic theory of Russian camps, noting Dallin's own admission of labor inefficiency.
Hannah Arendt cites Dallin's work as a source for statistics on the shortage of prison space in Russia in 1925–26.

book:web_4cd69ad8.description: A study of the Soviet forced labor camp system (Gulag) published by two Russian-born scholars and anti-communist writers.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt cites this book for statistics on forced labor and death rates in Russian labor camps.
Hannah Arendt lists this book as part of a bibliography or reference list.

book:web_20fee2f4.description: A seminal analysis of the political, economic, and social structure of Nazi Germany, arguing that Nazism represented a form of totalitarian monopoly capitalism and a collapse of the traditional state into a chaotic 'Behemoth'.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt cites Neumann's book as a reference for understanding the party-state relationship in totalitarian regimes.
Hannah Arendt quotes Neumann's work to illustrate a perspective on the nature of Nazi Germany.

book:web_649ff935.description: A collection of letters by T. E. Lawrence ('Lawrence of Arabia'), edited by David Garnett and published in 1939.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt cites Lawrence's letters, edited by Garnett, to provide an instance of 'pacification' methods in the Near East as described by Lawrence.
Hannah Arendt lists this book as part of a bibliography or reference list.

book:web_480e39dc.description: David Rousset's account of his experiences in Nazi concentration camps, originally published in French as 'L'Univers concentrationnaire' (1946). The English translation 'The Other Kingdom' was published in 1947 and was influential in documenting the concentration camp system.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt references Rousset's book in the context of discussing the protective wall of incredulity around Nazi atrocities.

book:web_8ef4f77c.description: A seminal work by French writer and political activist David Rousset, based on his own experience as a prisoner in Nazi concentration camps. It was one of the first detailed accounts of the camp system and won the Prix Renaudot in 1946.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt credits Rousset as the first to understand a particular aspect of the concentration camp phenomenon.
Hannah Arendt quotes Rousset's work to describe the incredulity of prisoners and outsiders regarding the horrors of concentration camps.
Hannah Arendt cites a specific page from Rousset's work for further detail.
Hannah Arendt cites Rousset's work to support the claim that life in a concentration camp was a prolonged process of dying.

book:web_fc1836b7.description: A scholarly study of Ernst Moritz Arndt's role in the German national awakening movement, published by Columbia University Press.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt cites Pundt's book as a source for information about Ernst Moritz Arndt and nationalism.
Hannah Arendt references Pundt's book as the source for a translation, though the excerpt is cut off.

book:web_572392c7.description: A book by Louis Dimier chronicling twenty years of the Action Française, a French monarchist and anti-republican movement.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt references Dimier's book as a source on attempts to win workers with antisemitic slogans and the actions of Léon Daudet.

book:web_5eeb3c09.description: A key ideological text of Nazi Germany, written by the party's chief ideologue Alfred Rosenberg. It promoted racist and antisemitic theories, arguing for the superiority of the 'Aryan' race and the need to combat 'Jewish influence.'
commentaries: Hannah Arendt references Rosenberg's book to contrast it with scholarly work, implying it is a work of charlatanism rather than genuine scholarship.

book:1946717.description: The Myth of the Twentieth Century (German: Der Mythus des zwanzigsten Jahrhunderts) by Alfred Rosenberg, one of the principal ideologues of the Nazi party and editor of the Nazi paper Volkischer Beobachter. It was the most influential Nazi text after Hitler's Mein Kampf. The titular "myth" is "the myth of blood, which under the sign of the swastika unchains the racial world-revolution. It is the awakening of the race soul, which after long sleep victoriously ends the race...
commentaries: Hannah Arendt critiques Rosenberg's book for its ideological error in admitting racial pluralism, which violated Nazi exclusionary principles.

book:web_4eb0296f.description: A biography of Friedrich Schleiermacher, the German theologian and philosopher, written by Wilhelm Dilthey. The work is considered an important contribution to intellectual history and biography.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt references Dilthey's biography of Schleiermacher as a prime source for understanding Jewish society in late 18th-century Berlin.

book:web_7f43a051.description: A biographical work about Georges Clemenceau, the French statesman, during his retirement years, written by journalist and writer René Benjamin.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt uses Benjamin's book to quote a remark by Clemenceau expressing his loss of faith in democracy.

book:web_3a2b30d8.description: A work by German colonial administrator and politician Heinrich Schnee, examining the relationship between nationalism and imperialism in the early 20th century.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt lists a book by Heinrich Schnee as part of a bibliography or reference list.

book:web_aa53a90d.description: A foundational Marxist analysis of capitalism, arguing that the fusion of banking and industrial capital into 'finance capital' leads to imperialism and the end of competitive capitalism.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt notes that Hilferding's book mentions, but does not fully analyze, imperialism's revival of primitive accumulation methods.
Hannah Arendt references Stalin's book as a source, citing a specific volume and chapter.
Hannah Arendt references Stalin's work 'Leninism' for his report denouncing deviations within the Party.

book:web_c36df213.description: A collection of speeches and writings by Joseph Stalin, originally published in Russian and later translated into English. The work presents Stalin's interpretation and application of Marxist-Leninist theory.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt lists several books by J. V. Stalin as part of a bibliography or reference list.
Hannah Arendt cites a statement by Stalin, likely from a speech or written work, to illustrate the scale of promotions following purges in the Soviet Union.

book:2226120.description: Originally published 1934, a collection of articles and speeches on the nationalities question in the Soviet Union. Before the 1917 revolution, Stalin was the Communist Party's expert on the "nationalities problem"; after the revolution he became Commissar for the Nationalities in the early years of the Soviet Union. The nationalities problem was a debate over which national groups of the old Russian Empire were to remain a part of the new Soviet Union and which should form independent nations. The material...

book:web_a325b00f.description: A brief and reliable account of the Dreyfus Affair and its impact on the French Third Republic, published in 1930.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt describes Charensol's work as brief and reliable.
Hannah Arendt references G. Charensol's work on the complicity of the Haute Banque in the Orleanist movement.

book:web_dbd13333.description: A collection of Stalin's writings and speeches on Leninism, published in English translation in London in 1933.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt lists several books by J. V. Stalin as part of a bibliography or reference list.

book:1423460.description: Voltaire, avec son esprit acerbe et sa plume subtile, a trouve dans la forme du dictionnaire une voie royale d'expression qui lui permis d'echapper a la censure de son temps. Utilisant le jeu des renvois entre les definitions pour tromper la vigilance des autorites et inserant ses analyses les plus iconoclastes dans la definition de termes anodins, Voltaire se livre a un jeu de piste a l'attention d'un lecteur averti, incite a concevoir ce dictionnaire comme un veritable rebus. Ainsi, a l'article Idolatrie,...
commentaries: Hannah Arendt notes Voltaire's entry in his philosophical dictionary regarding racial differences.

book:1362044.description: Candidenous conte les mesaventures d'un voyageur philosophe qui affronte les horreurs de la guerre et les sanglants caprices de la Nature ; qui connait les desillusions de l'amour et decouvre les turpitudes de ses semblables, faisant a l'occasion l'experience de leurs dangereuses fantaisies. Pourtant si l'homme est un bien mechant animal et si l'existence n'est qu'une cascade de catastrophes, est-ce une raison pour que le heros perde sa serenite et le recit de son allegresse ? Sous la forme d'une ironique f...
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges references Faguet's critique that Flaubert was influenced by memories of characters from Voltaire's 'Candide'.
Susan Sontag cites Voltaire's 'Candide' as a conscious literary reference influencing her own first novel, seen as a satire on optimism.
Northrop Frye contrasts Voltaire's Candide with Rousseau's Emile to illustrate a shift from the novel to another form of fiction.
Erich Auerbach cites Voltaire's 'Candide' as a work that polemically attacks Leibniz's metaphysical optimism.

book:web_d3addb47.description: A philosophical tale by Voltaire, first published in 1768, telling the story of the Babylonian princess Formosante and her quest to find her destined husband.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges cites Voltaire's 'La Princesse de Babylone' as a book that influenced Beckford, based on Chapman's research.

book:web_37fa0cfe.description: Voltaire's biography of King Charles XII of Sweden, first published in 1731. It is considered one of the foundational works of modern historical writing, blending narrative with philosophical reflection.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Voltaire's history of Charles XII as a source for a historical analogy.

book:web_894f653f.description: Historical work by Voltaire about the reign of Louis XIV of France, considered one of the first modern histories with critical analysis of sources and emphasis on cultural achievements alongside political events.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Voltaire's history to compare the size of the Roman military establishment with that of a modern European monarchy.

book:web_345e5b6a.description: A pamphlet by Talleyrand, written in 1799, advocating for the establishment of new colonies. It was later reprinted in the 'Annales' of the Académie des Sciences Coloniales in 1929.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt lists a work by C. M. de Talleyrand as part of a bibliography or reference list.

book:392274.description: "Youth" is an autobiographical short story by Joseph Conrad. Written in 1898, it was first published in Blackwood's Magazine, and included as the first story in the 1902 volume Youth, a Narrative, and Two Other Stories. This volume also includes Heart of Darkness and The End of the Tether, stories concerned with the themes of maturity and old age, respectively. "Youth" depicts a young man's first journey to the East. It is narrated by Charles Marlow who is also the narrator of Lord Jim and Chance. The narra...
commentaries: Hannah Arendt describes Conrad's work as the most illuminating on race experience in Africa.
Hannah Arendt cites Joseph Conrad's phrase to characterize the scramble for Africa and investment fever.
Hannah Arendt references Conrad's ideas to describe the isolated and lawless existence of the Boers, using his imagery to underscore their detachment from civilized society.

book:12984120.description: Heyst was not conscious of either friends or of enemies. It was the very essence of his life to be a solitary achievement, accomplished not by hermit-like withdrawal with its silence and immobility, but by a system of restless wandering, by the detachment of an impermanent dweller amongst changing scenes.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges quotes Joseph Conrad's statement about the reality of a character in his novel Victory to illustrate how novelists typically believe in their characters, contrasting this with Hawthorne's method.

book:86658.description:
Mr Verloc, the secret agent, keeps a shop in London's Soho where he lives with his wife Winnie, her infirm mother, and her idiot brother, Stevie. When Verloc is reluctantly involved in an anarchist plot to blow up the Greenwich Observatory things go disastrously wrong, and what appears to be "a simple tale" proves to involve politicians, policemen, foreign diplomats and London's fashionable society in the darkest and most surprising interrelations.
Based on the text which Conrad's first English readers enjo...
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges notes that the director claims the film was inspired by Joseph Conrad's novel.
Jorge Luis Borges cites a specific passage from Conrad's novel to argue against Hitchcock's interpretation of the character.

book:115467.description: Chance was Conrad's first commercial success after nearly twenty years as a writer, & his first novel to have a happy ending. It tells the story of Flora de Barral, the abandoned daughter of a bankrupt tycoon, & her long struggle to find happiness & dignity.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges notes Conrad's use of a non-chronological narrative technique in his novel Chance, comparing it to the structure of Citizen Kane.

book:3537012.description: Many chronicles have been written about life at sea, but few, if any, can compare with Joseph Conrad's masterpiece. It is the story of one unremarkable steamship captain, pitted against a storm of incredible fury. Captain Macwhirr has a reputation as a solid, steadfast man, who "having just enough imagination to carry him through each successive day, and no more" cannot fully believe any storm would be a match for his powerful ship. So, when the barometer and other clues begin to hint at trouble ahead, he i...
commentaries: Umberto Eco references Conrad's original work through Gide's French translation to illustrate challenges in translating idiomatic expressions and the tension between foreignising and domesticating strategies.

book:1427357.description:
This immortal novel of the sea tells the story of a British sailor haunted by a single youthful act of cowardly betrayal. To the white men in Bombay, Calcutta, and Rangoon, Jim is a man of mystery. To the primitive natives deep in the Malayan jungle, he is a god gifted with supernatural powers. To the beautiful half-caste girl who flees to his hut for protection, he is a lord to be feared and loved.
Lord Jim--Conrad's classic portrait of a man's guilt, his search for forgiveness, and his final, tragic redem...
commentaries: Northrop Frye lists this novel as an example of a work that parodies romance conventions.

book:780681.description: 'Nostromo'--though nearly one hundred years old--says as much about today's Latin America as any of the finest recent accounts of that region's turbulent political life.
commentaries: Northrop Frye cites this novel as a modern example in the tradition of romance centered on the quest for buried treasure.

book:web_a5718ce0.description: A critical study on the formation of racial doctrine in the 18th century and its expansion in the 19th century, published in Brussels.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt lists a book by Théophile Simar as part of a bibliography or reference list.
Hannah Arendt cites Simar's book to correct the misconception that François Hotman was a forerunner of racial doctrines.

book:web_b49bf6a5.description: Historical biography of Joseph Süß Oppenheimer (1698-1738), a Jewish financier and court Jew in Württemberg who was executed and became a controversial figure in German history.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt references Stern's book for specific page details.

book:web_e84b7c0b.description: An 8-volume collection of documents and evidence compiled for the Nuremberg Trials. Volume VII contains the article 'On Dachau and Buchenwald' by Bruno Bettelheim, which is a reprint of his 1943 article 'Individual and Mass Behavior in Extreme Situations' based on his 1938-1939 imprisonment.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt cites Bettelheim's report as one of the best accounts of Nazi concentration camps.
Hannah Arendt cites Bettelheim's observations on the psychological impact of nonsensical tasks on new prisoners.
Hannah Arendt cites Bettelheim's observation on the shared unreal attitude between camp guards and prisoners.

book:1229870.description: An objective and documentary history of the earliest origins and formative years of the Workers-Peasants Red Army from the Civil War to the initial disasters of the war with Germany, the Great Patriotic War, culminating in the "battle for Moscow" in November-December 1941.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt lists this book as part of a bibliography or reference list.

book:web_e6ed77b0.description: A study of the Gestapo (Geheime Staatspolizei), the secret state police of Nazi Germany, examining its organization, methods, and role in the Nazi regime.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt lists this book as part of a bibliography or reference list.

book:3082766.description: Als dreissigjahriger Jurist wurde Henry Picker, dessen Eltern mit Hitler seit den zwanziger Jahren bekannt waren, im Marz 1942 ins Fuhrerhauptquartier berufen, wo ihn Hitler zu seinem "standigen Tischgast" bestimmte. So erlangte Picker Einblick in Hitlers Werdegang, Gedankenwelt, Politik und Kriegsfuhrung. Seine Niederschriften der "Tischgesprache" Hitlers halten mit der Unbestechlichkeit des historisch, politisch und juristisch geschulten Beobachters fest, wie sich Hitler im Kreis seiner Mitarbeiter gab, w...
commentaries: Hannah Arendt cites Hitler's table talks as a source for his strategic intentions regarding Bolshevism and the West.
Hannah Arendt references this book of Hitler's conversations as a source for understanding his social influence and ideological consistency.
Hannah Arendt cites Hitler's table talks to reveal his private mockery of pan-Germanic ideology and his shift to 'Aryan' racial thinking.
Hannah Arendt cites Hitler's table talks to illustrate his racial ideology and concept of world conquest.

book:web_88523ccd.description: Gottfried Feder's exposition of the Nazi Party's 25-point program, which he helped draft. Feder was a key early Nazi ideologue and economic theorist.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt mentions Feder's program in the context of its limited role within the Nazi movement despite its prominence in literature.

book:7752801.description: This is a pre-1923 historical reproduction that was curated for quality. Quality assurance was conducted on each of these books in an attempt to remove books with imperfections introduced by the digitization process. Though we have made best efforts - the books may have occasional errors that do not impede the reading experience. We believe this work is culturally important and have elected to bring the book back into print as part of our continuing commitment to the preservation of printed works worldwide.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt introduces Gobineau's 'Essai sur l'Inégalité des Races Humaines' as a foundational text for race theories, noting its later influence.

book:web_c87c7252.description: A highly influential sociological work arguing that religious belief, rather than reason, is the driving force behind social progress and cohesion. It was a bestseller that sparked widespread debate in the 1890s.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt references Kidd's book as a key text in social Darwinism.

book:web_e1911834.description: A study of race-thinking and its relationship to the state, published in Germany in 1933. It is considered a key early work analyzing racial ideology within political theory.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt describes this book as the best historical account of race-thinking in the pattern of a 'history of ideas'.

book:web_51dc5e74.description: The authoritative multi-volume biography of British Prime Minister Benjamin Disraeli, begun by Monypenny and completed after his death by Buckle.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt cites Monypenny and Buckle's work as a source for information about Disraeli.
Hannah Arendt references Monypenny and Buckle's work in the context of discussing Disraeli.
Hannah Arendt cites Monypenny and Buckle's work regarding Robert Cecil's article in the Quarterly Review.
Hannah Arendt references Monypenny and Buckle's work in relation to Disraeli.
Hannah Arendt cites Monypenny and Buckle's biography for an evaluation of Disraeli's triumph, including a quote from Tennyson's In Memoriam.
Hannah Arendt references a specific volume and book within Monypenny and Buckle's work.

book:web_8697f281.description: A political analysis by Peter Drucker examining the failure of established political systems and the rise of fascism and totalitarianism in Europe.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt lists this book as part of a bibliography or reference list.

book:web_6893902f.description: A collection of speeches by Adolf Hitler during the early period of World War II, published by the Nazi Party's central publishing house (Zentralverlag der NSDAP, Franz Eher Nachfolger).
commentaries: Hannah Arendt references a collection of Hitler's wartime speeches to show his belief in extracting the 'worthwhile' men from the German nation.
Hannah Arendt cites Hitler's work to explain the distinction between propaganda and organization within the Nazi movement.

book:54270.description: Madman, tyrant, animal - history has given Adolf Hitler many names. In Mein Kampf (My Struggle), often called the Nazi bible, Hitler describes his life, frustrations, ideals, and dreams. Born to an impoverished couple in a small town in Austria, the young Adolf grew up with the fervent desire to become a painter. The death of his parents and outright rejection from art schools in Vienna forced him into underpaid work as a labourer. During the First World War, Hitler served in the infantry and was decorated....
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Mein Kampf as the definitive ideological text of Nazism, contrasting its systematic philosophy with the ideological incoherence of Italian Fascism.
Umberto Eco cites Hitler’s Mein Kampf as a later, racially charged extension of antisemitic tropes, linking Jewish appearance to moral and social corruption.

book:web_c0d9dd45.description: A two-volume sociological study of colonialism by French sociologist and colonial administrator René Maunier, published in Paris in 1932.

book:web_2493f112.description: A historical work about German colonial struggles in Africa, written by the son of colonial governor Theodor Leutwein.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt cites Leutwein's book alongside Townsend's, likely for additional perspective on colonial struggles in Africa.

book:web_713a5d77.description: A political pamphlet by journalist Otto Glagau (1834-1892) criticizing the National Liberal Party in Germany and advocating for conservative reaction, published during the Anti-Socialist Law era.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt references Glagau's book as an antisemitic publication from the period.

book:web_c57c442a.description: An influential antisemitic pamphlet published in 1876, attacking Jewish financiers and speculators during the German economic boom (Gründerzeit). Originally appeared as a series of articles in the magazine 'Die Gartenlaube' before being published as a book.

book:web_d798ff69.description: A scholarly analysis of French right-wing politics and their relationship with Nazi Germany during the interwar period, published during World War II.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt cites Micaud's book as providing a careful analysis of the political stance of the French Right towards Nazi Germany in the interwar period.
