book:web_b04a57b0.description: Major philosophical work by Nicholas of Cusa (Nicolaus Cusanus) presenting his concept of 'learned ignorance' and exploring the relationship between God, the universe, and human knowledge through mathematical metaphors.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges cites this book for its mathematical conjectures about infinity, considering it for inclusion in a planned history of the infinite.
Frances A. Yates states that Agrippa certainly had in mind the philosophical statement of the theme found in this work.
Umberto Eco cites Nicholas of Cusa's De docta ignorantia as a foundational philosophical source for the idea that God, as absolute, is fundamentally unknowable and beyond human conceptualization.

book:web_8fc9a1d1.description: A theological and philosophical treatise by Nicholas of Cusa, also known as 'The Vision of God', exploring mystical theology and the relationship between God and humanity.
commentaries: Joseph Campbell references a theological work by Nicholas of Cusa, as cited in a paper by Coomaraswamy.

book:web_49edf222.description: A work on universal language by Spanish physician, journalist, and writer Pedro Mata, who also wrote medical texts and novels. This book proposes a system for universal communication.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges references Dr. Pedro Mata's book as the source where he found a census of words from Bonifacio Sotos Ochando's universal language.

book:4470418.description: This is a reproduction of a book published before 1923. This book may have occasional imperfections such as missing or blurred pages, poor pictures, errant marks, etc. that were either part of the original artifact, or were introduced by the scanning process. We believe this work is culturally important, and despite the imperfections, have elected to bring it back into print as part of our continuing commitment to the preservation of printed works worldwide. We appreciate your understanding of the imperfect...
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges notes Galland's 'Mille et une nuits' as a controversial yet admirable influence on Beckford.

book:200299.description: Inspired in Don Segundo Ramirez, a cattle drover Ricardo Guiraldes met personally and whose tomb lies in San Antonio de Areco, very close to the author's own, don Segundo Sombra more than a novel is a lesson on the gaucho lifestyle. Ricardo Guiraldes, a friend of Jorge Luis Borges -they both founded the legendary magazine Proa- managed to develop a simple and modern language, a high quality mixture of literacy and colourful local camp expressions that earned him a major standing among the best representativ...
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges criticizes Güiraldes's 'Don Segundo Sombra' for exaggerating mundane tasks, unlike Hudson's naturalistic descriptions in 'The Purple Land'.
Jorge Luis Borges cites Güiraldes's novel as an idealized portrayal of gaucho life.

book:1639333.description: Es el texto mas celebre de Espronceda. El personaje de Felix de Montemar, de personalidad faustica, se inspira en la leyenda de don Juan Tenorio. Terrorifico relato en el que se percibe la influencia de Lord Byron y de la novela gotica inglesa. El heroe desafia a los poderes divinos.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges references Espronceda's narrative poem as an example of the Don Juan literary tradition.

book:web_e10b9cfe.description: A major work on optics, light, shadow, and projection by Jesuit scholar Athanasius Kircher, featuring descriptions of magic lanterns, camera obscura, sundials, and other optical devices.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges cites Kircher's 'Ars magna lucis et umbrae' as the source for an invention resembling the magic lantern, linking it to early cinematic technology.

book:web_9bd7498f.description: A 17th-century scholarly work by Jesuit polymath Athanasius Kircher that uses physics and mathematics to argue that the Tower of Babel could not have reached heaven, blending theology, linguistics, and early scientific reasoning.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Kircher's Turris Babel as an instance of applying mathematical reasoning to a biblical narrative, revealing the intersection of science and myth in early modern thought.

book:web_bcda30c8.description: A 1660 cosmological work by Jesuit scholar Athanasius Kircher, presenting various models of the solar system, including the Copernican system, alongside mythological and ancient systems. It reflects the scientific and theological tensions of the 17th century.
commentaries: Umberto Eco references Kircher’s book to illustrate the tension between traditional and emerging cosmological models, highlighting Kircher’s rejection of Copernicanism despite his detailed presentation of it.

book:web_aa1f624b.description: A comprehensive 17th-century work by Jesuit scholar Athanasius Kircher on the hidden structures and phenomena of the Earth, including volcanoes, fossils, and subterranean waters. It blends scientific observation with speculative natural philosophy.
commentaries: Umberto Eco references Kircher's work as an example of pre-scientific but earnest attempts to explain natural phenomena through observation and imaginative theory.

book:web_284ccfd1.description: A major work of metaphysical idealism by British philosopher F. H. Bradley, arguing that reality is a single, absolute, and all-inclusive whole, while ordinary experience reveals only appearances.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges discusses Bradley's 'Appearance and Reality' as a work that denies all relations, leading to an infinite regress when considering how terms are connected.
Jorge Luis Borges references F. H. Bradley's work 'Appearance and Reality' to advance the critique of time's divisibility and existence.
Jorge Luis Borges references Bradley's book to discuss his observations on the nature of the present and time.

book:8160517.description: Premier roman de Leon Bloy, Le Desespere (1887) est un pave dans la mare de tous les conformismes. Cain Marchenoir est le heros de ce roman largement autobiographique : catholique intransigeant revolte par le silence de Dieu et la vaine attente de la redemption, paria parmi les hommes, il lance le plus violent des anathemes contre ses contemporains. Le Desespere est tout a la fois un cri de revolte, un amoureux blaspheme, un pamphlet vitriole contre la foule des <>republicains et la <>des lettres. Mais Le D...
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges directs the reader to Bloy's novel as an example where a specific Kabbalistic conjecture is developed.
Jorge Luis Borges cites a story from this book as an example of a narrative resembling Kafka's work, specifically about characters who never leave their hometown.

book:677058.description: In the early years of the thirteenth century the Danish writer Saxo Grammaticus provided his people with a History of the Danes, an account of their glorious past from the legendary kings and heroes of Denmark to the historical present. It is one of the major sources for the heroic and mythological traditions of northern Europe, though the complex Latin style and the wide range of material brought together from different sources have limited its use. Here Hilda Ellis Davidson, a specialist in Scandinavian m...
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges quotes from Saxo Grammaticus's 'Gesta Danorum' to support his point about Icelandic historians impartially recording history.

book:web_68b2a577.description: A pioneering encyclopedia of Islamic, Middle Eastern, and Asian history, geography, and culture, compiled by the French orientalist Barthélemy d'Herbelot. It was a major reference work for European scholars of the Orient throughout the 18th and 19th centuries.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges lists d'Herbelot's 'Bibliotheque orientale' as one of the works that influenced Beckford, according to his biographer Chapman.

book:web_2a7c2ba6.description: Massive encyclopedia of Islamic, Persian, Turkish, and other Eastern knowledge, compiled by French orientalist d'Herbelot. First major European reference work on Islamic civilization.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references D'Herbelot's work as a source on Artaxerxes' lineage, specifically the entry for Ardshir.

book:352047.description:
J.W. Dunne (1866-1949) was an accomplished English aeronautical engineer and a designer of Britian's early military aircraft. His An Experiment with Time, first published in 1927, sparked a great deal of scientific interest in--and controversy about--his new model of multidimensional time.
A series of strange, troubling precognitive dreams (including a vision of the then future catastrophic eruption of Mt. Pelee on the island of Martininque in 1902) led Dunne to re-evaluate the meaning and significance of d...
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges references a specific chapter in Dunne's book 'An Experiment with Time' to outline his argument on consciousness.
Jorge Luis Borges cites Dunne's book to discuss a concept of perpendicular time, referencing a specific chapter.

book:94486.description:
Jorge Luis Borges declared The Invention of Morela masterpiece of plotting, comparable to The Turn of the Screwand Journey to the Center of the Earth. Set on a mysterious island, Bioy's novella is a story of suspense and exploration, as well as a wonderfully unlikely romance, in which every detail is at once crystal clear and deeply mysterious.
Inspired by Bioy Casares's fascination with the movie star Louise Brooks, The Invention of Morelhas gone on to live a secret life of its own. Greatly admired by Juli...
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges introduces Bioy Casares' novel as the subject of discussion, highlighting its plot and significance.
Jorge Luis Borges again references Bioy Casares' novel, placing it among other works with admirable plots.

book:web_1750656e.description: An English translation and study of the Chinese Taoist philosopher Zhuangzi (Chuang Tzu) by the British diplomat and sinologist Herbert Allen Giles. This was the first complete English translation of the Zhuangzi text.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges references Giles's book as the source for the story of Chuang Tzu's dream.

book:web_9f8f8c04.description: One of the Canterbury Tales, a collection of stories written in Middle English by Geoffrey Chaucer in the late 14th century. The Franklin's Tale explores themes of marriage, honor, and generosity.
commentaries: Northrop Frye cites The Franklin's Tale as an example of mature innocent wisdom in a contemplative, erotic world.

book:2339726.description: On a spring day in April--sometime in the waning years of the 14th century--29 travelers set out for Canterbury on a pilgrimage to the shrine of Saint Thomas Beckett. Among them is a knight, a monk, a prioress, a plowman, a miller, a merchant, a clerk, and an oft-widowed wife from Bath. Travel is arduous and wearing; to maintain their spirits, this band of pilgrims entertains each other with a series of tall tales that span the spectrum of literary genres. Five hundred years later, people are still reading....
commentaries: Harold Bloom identifies Chaucer as Shakespeare's truest precursor, specifically referencing his work 'Canterbury Tales' as the source of the literary debt for the character Falstaff.
Harold Bloom lists this work as one of the few more essential to the Western Canon than Paradise Lost.

book:13503979.description: The Finnegans Wake Notebook Edition is a fully integrated and cross-referenced edition of all the extant work-books compiled by Joyce after the completion of Ulysses. It will be published as a series of fascicles, one per authorial notebook, three per scribal notebook, fifty-five in all. This will make individual notebooks available to scholars as they appear and allow critical feedback, laying the foundations for an electronic edition that will be prepared simultaneously. The editorial aim is to bring toge...
commentaries: Umberto Eco references Joyce's work as a key example of culturally embedded text requiring radical translational adaptation.
Umberto Eco references Finnegans Wake as the source text embodying linguistic fragmentation and multilingual play, central to Joyce's translational philosophy.
Umberto Eco cites Finnegans Wake to argue that its dense intertextuality demands an informed reading, distinguishing it from the accessible duality of double coding.
Jorge Luis Borges mentions Joyce's 'Finnegans Wake' as an even more demanding and incomprehensible work than 'Ulysses', whose readers are deemed inconceivable.
Jorge Luis Borges references Joyce's work as an example of literary experimentation with time and simultaneity.
Harold Bloom notes that Joyce used Vico's ideas in structuring his book, and that he himself is following Joyce's example.
Harold Bloom contrasts the effect of Beckett's 'Endgame' on interpreting Shakespeare with the lack of such effect from Joyce's major novels, which are saturated with Shakespeare.
Harold Bloom compares 'Finnegans Wake' to 'Faust, Part Two', noting its humor and Harold Bloom's good faith.
Joseph Campbell quotes a passage from Joyce's book to illustrate a philosophical concept.
Joseph Campbell attributes the term 'monomyth' to this specific book by James Joyce.
Susan Sontag presents this book as a unique counter-example to the idea that anything can be translated, arguing its multilingual nature makes it untranslatable.

book:15956695.description: 'Ulysses', one of the greatest novels of the 20th century, has had a profound influence on modern fiction. In a series of episodes covering the course of a single day, 16 June 1904, the novel traces the movements of Leopold Bloom and Stephen Dedalus through the streets of Dublin.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges references T.S. Eliot's review of 'Ulysses' to support the idea of new literature being based on old myths.
Jorge Luis Borges cites Joyce's novel as the prime example of a work where every detail is a prophecy, illustrating a magical causal procedure.
Jorge Luis Borges references Joyce's novel 'Ulysses' as a work that demands extraordinary cognitive abilities to read, comparing its reader to the fictional character Funes.
Jorge Luis Borges references Joyce's novel in the title of an essay, noting Borges's claim about being an early Spanish-speaking reader.
Umberto Eco references Joyce's Ulysses as an example of spatial representation through detailed listing, linking it to the rhetorical concept of hypotyposis.
Umberto Eco references Joyce’s Ulysses to contrast double coding with deliberate allegorical structure, noting that Joyce provides clear cues for the dual reading.
Susan Sontag suggests that Döblin drew inspiration from Joyce's Ulysses for Berlin Alexanderplatz.

Susan Sontag mentions this book as an example of a challenging text that is often cited in arguments about translatability, implying it is a work for which the claim 'anything can be translated' is tested.
Northrop Frye cites Joyce's 'Ulysses', specifically the 'Sirens' episode, as evidence of elaborate experiments in prose melos with a musical analogy.
Harold Bloom mentions Joyce's novel 'Ulysses' as a work that Anthony Burgess's novel repeats without creatively revising, in contrast to Beckett's misreading of it.
Harold Bloom references Joyce's Ulysses and its character Leopold Bloom as an example of a persuasively complete person in fiction.
Harold Bloom notes Woolf's negative judgment of Joyce's novel.
Harold Bloom contrasts the effect of Beckett's 'Endgame' on interpreting Shakespeare with the lack of such effect from Joyce's major novels, which are saturated with Shakespeare.
Erich Auerbach cites Ulysses as a prime example of a work filled with universal doom, cynicism, and uninterpretable symbolism, reflecting the confusion of the post-World War I era.
Joseph Campbell cites a passage from James Joyce's 'Ulysses' to support a concept of androgynous, self-sufficient glorified man.
Umberto Eco references Joyce's Ulysses as a controversial and poorly received work, criticizing its style and dismissing it as not a work of art.

book:web_72f93aa2.description: A collection of James Joyce's Italian writings, edited by Jacqueline Risset, including texts produced in collaboration with Nino Frank, originally published in 1979 by Mondadori in Milan. The volume compiles Joyce's journalistic and literary pieces written in Italian, primarily from the 1930s.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites this collected edition of Joyce's Italian writings as a source for historical translation variants of 'Anna Livia Plurabella'.

book:103800.description: Portrays Stephen Dedalus' Dublin childhood and youth, his quest for identity through art and his gradual emancipation from the claims of family, religion and Ireland itself.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Joyce's earlier novel to support the claim that his literary style deteriorates into incoherence and fragmentation.
Umberto Eco cites Joyce's novel as the starting point of his perceived artistic decline and rejection of national spirit.

Umberto Eco references Joyce's novel to illustrate Aristotle's conception of God as detached and transcendent, using the literary image to reinforce a philosophical argument about divine immanence and distance.
Umberto Eco lists this novel as a published work, indicating it is referenced as a literary source.
Umberto Eco references Joyce’s novel to illustrate the momentary illumination of beauty and its isolating effect on the individual.
David Foster Wallace cites Joyce’s novel as a landmark work that profoundly affected him.
Umberto Eco cites Joyce's novel as a source for a quoted passage used in a comparative table.
Northrop Frye cites a specific idea from Joyce's novel 'A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man' to characterize the lyric.
Harold Bloom alludes to Joyce's A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man as a comparative benchmark for an artist's formative work.
Joseph Campbell cites a specific page from Joyce's novel.

book:997958.description: Stephen Hero is a posthumously-published autobiographical novel by Irish author James Joyce. Its published form reflects only a portion of an original manuscript, part of which was lost. Many of its ideas were used in composing A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Joyce's Stephen Hero to define epiphany as a spiritual moment, and notes its recurring fiery imagery in Joyce’s works as an extension of D’Annunzio’s aesthetic fire.

book:408862.description: Before Joseph Campbell became the world's most famous practitioner of comparative mythology, there was Sir James George Frazer. The Golden Boughwas originally published in two volumes in 1890, but Frazer became so enamored of his topic that over the next few decades he expanded the work sixfold, then in 1922 cut it all down to a single thick edition suitable for mass distribution. The thesis on the origins of magic and religion that it elaborates "will be long and laborious," Frazer warns readers, "but may....
commentaries: Northrop Frye cites Frazer's work as a key text for understanding the ritual content of naive drama, noting its influence on literary criticism despite being an anthropological study.
Joseph Campbell cites Frazer's work as an example of an exhaustive, evidence-heavy scholarly manner that he is deliberately not emulating.
Joseph Campbell references Frazer's work as a source on ritual regicide and mythological traditions.
Joseph Campbell states that Frazer's work provides extensive description and discussion of the preceding topics.
Joseph Campbell directly quotes from this work, using it as a source for mythological or folkloric information.
Joseph Campbell quotes Frazer's explanation of the taboo against sacred persons touching the ground, using it as a theoretical framework for the preceding ethnographic example.
Joseph Campbell cites Frazer as a representative of the intellectual interpretation of mythology as a primitive explanation of nature.
Joseph Campbell extensively cites Sir James G. Frazer's work, particularly noting his interpretation of mythology and his analysis of the foot taboo.
Joseph Campbell begins a comparative citation from Frazer's work regarding the conception of a Dying and Reviving God.

book:web_1a673591.description: A novel by English author Eden Phillpotts, published in 1934. Phillpotts (1862-1960) was a prolific writer of novels, plays, and poetry, best known for his Dartmoor-based works.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges references Phillpotts' work as another example of a detective novel with psychological elements.

book:web_8de3518f.description: A scholarly work on the Eleatic school of pre-Socratic philosophy, focusing on Parmenides, Zeno, and Melissus. Albertelli was an Italian philosopher and anti-fascist resistance fighter.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges references Albertelli's book 'Gli Eleati' as a source for interpreting Parmenides' concept of the sphere.

book:web_b335d4cb.description: An epic poem in continuation of Ariosto's 'Orlando Furioso', focusing on the character Angelica. The work is often referred to simply as 'Angélica'. Canto XI is referenced in Borges's text.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges references Barahona de Soto's epic poem as another example of the paradoxical syllogism structure.

book:web_16174475.description: An essay or short work by Hilaire Belloc, likely included in one of his collections, where he discusses William Beckford and compares his prose to Voltaire's.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges cites Belloc's book for its opinion on Beckford, comparing his prose to Voltaire's and condemning his character.

book:30231779.description: Considered by Rumi to be "the master" of Sufi mystic poetry, Attar is best known for his epic poem The Conference of the Birds, a magnificent allegorical tale about the soul's search for meaning. The poem recounts the perilous journey of the world's birds to the faraway peaks of Mount Qaf--a mythical mountain that wraps around the earth--in search of their king, the mysterious Simorgh. Attar's beguiling anecdotes and humor intermingle the sublime with the mundane, the spiritual with the worldly, and the rel...
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges lists Attar's literary works, including the Conference of the Birds, which contains the Simurgh legend.
Jorge Luis Borges cites Attar's 'Conference of the Birds' as an example of a narrative about unity, contrasting it with Stevenson's dualism.
Jorge Luis Borges references the Persian poet Attar and his work 'The Conference of the Birds' to illustrate the principle of identity where the seekers become what they seek.
Jorge Luis Borges discusses Attar as the creator of the Simurgh in the Conference of the Birds, noting his life and works.

book:web_cab95509.description: A foundational work on Buddhism by German Buddhist scholar Georg Grimm, presenting Buddhist doctrine and philosophy.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges references Grimm's book on Buddhist teachings to explain the process of eliminating the self, noting its excellence.

book:157118.description:
Throughout history philosophers have sought to define, understand, and delineate concepts important to human well-being. One such concept is "knowledge." Many philosophers believed that absolute, certain knowledge, is possible--that the physical world and ideas formulated about it could be given solid foundation unaffected by the varieties of mere opinion.
Sextus Empiricus stands as an example of the "skeptic" school of thought whose members believed that knowledge was either unattainable or, if a genuine p...
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges cites Sextus Empiricus's 'Hypotyposes' as an example of using infinite regression to argue against the validity of definitions.

book:551371.description:
'The Argonauts were terrified at the sight. But Jason planting his feet apart stood to receive them, as a reef in the sea confronts the tossing billows in a gale.'
The tragic, epic love affair that allowed Jason to get the Golden Fleece.
Introducing Little Black Classics: 80 books for Penguin's 80th birthday. Little Black Classics celebrate the huge range and diversity of Penguin Classics, with books from around the world and across many centuries. They take us from a balloon ride over Victorian London to a...
commentaries: Joseph Campbell directs the reader to a specific book of Apollonios of Rhodes's epic poem for an account of a flight.
Umberto Eco cites Apollonius of Rhodes’s epic as a classical source of island legends, linking it to the mythic tradition of inaccessible lands.

book:2506738.description: Juan Moreira fue publicado por La Patria Argentina en forma de folletin del 28 de noviembre de 1879 al 8 de enero de 1880. Se trata de la obra mas conocida de Eduardo Gutierrez y una de las cumbres del romanticismo literario latinoamericano. Esta novela por entregas, inspirada en una cronica policial que explicaba la muerte de un gaucho, obtuvo un exito enorme e inmediato entre los lectores. Cuatro anos despues, Gutierrez reescribio su obra como "microdrama" para ser representada en el circo. Ha sido llevad...
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges mentions Gutierrez's gaucho novels and Borges's comparison to Cooper.
Harold Bloom references Santayana's book to discuss his categorization of poets and his views on Dante's love and Platonism.

book:19554254.description: And to be true, and speak my soul, when I survey the occurrences of my life, and call into account the Finger of GOD, I can perceive nothing but an abyss and mass of mercies, either in general to mankind, or in particular to my self. And (whether out of the prejudice of my affection, or an inverting and partial conceit of His mercies, I know not; but) those which others term crosses, afflictions, judgements, misfortunes, to me, who inquire farther into them then their visible effects, they both appear, and....
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges cites Browne's book to introduce the theme of the navel and original sin, which connects to the subsequent discussion of Gosse.
Jorge Luis Borges notes that Sir Thomas Browne used the same metaphor as Pascal in 'Religio Medici' to describe divinity.
Jorge Luis Borges cites Browne's 'Religio Medici' as a source confirming the metaphor of nature as a divine book.

book:8166045.description: Urn Burial, one of the most influential essays in Western literature, is now available as a New Directions Pearl. Hydriotaphia, or Urn Burial, is one of the pinnacles of Renaissance scholarship and without doubt one of the great essays in English literature. Beginning with observations on the recent discovery of Roman antiquities in the form of burial urns, Browne's associative mind wanders to elephant graveyards, to pre-Christian cremation ceremonies, and finally to the idea of Christian burial. Browne the...
commentaries: Northrop Frye cites Browne's 'Urn Burial' as an example of a prose work that functions as a rhetorical exercise with recurring rhythmic units.

book:web_b971071d.description: A narrative poem by William Morris retelling the story of Jason and the Argonauts.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges uses this book as a primary example to analyze narrative techniques, specifically focusing on Morris's method of making mythical elements believable.

book:784860.description: A new critical edition of a literary masterpieceA farsighted Victorian, William Morris was a pioneering socialist, book designer and decorative artist, founder of the Society for the Protection of Ancient Buildings, and author of intense short lyrics, long poetic narratives, and utopian-socialist prose romances. This annotated critical edition is the first attempt to make Morris's 42,000 word verse sequence accessible to a modern audience. The edition's scholarly apparatus also records the location of extan...
commentaries: Northrop Frye describes The Earthly Paradise as a very pure example of the contemplative phase where old men interchange myths in a dreamlike land.

book:716523.description: This book was converted from its physical edition to the digital format by a community of volunteers. You may find it for free on the web. Purchase of the Kindle edition includes wireless delivery.
commentaries: Northrop Frye references The Sundering Flood as an example where a dividing river symbolizes a sexual barrier.

book:24357337.description:
Wilkie Collins's enthralling story of the cursed diamond stolen from an Indian shrine is the first and probably finest work of detective fiction in the language.
The exquisite Moonstone, a diamond that brings bad luck to whoever has it in their possession, is given to Rachel Verinder for her eighteenth birthday. To the dismay of her family, it is stolen from her that very same night. Sergeant Cuff is brought in to investigate and, with the help of Gabriel Betteredge, the family steward, he becomes aware of....
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges cites Collins' novel as an example of a detective story that verges on psychological fiction.

book:5891.description: Mistaken identities, locked rooms, madness, and romance--these are a few of the ingredients the author (one of the most successful and popular Victorian writers) used to inspire "the 'creepy' effect, as of pounded ice dropped down the back," that, according to one of his friends, was Wilkie Collins's aim in writing The Woman in White. Popularly regarded as one of the author's finest works, and widely copied by other writers, this thriller was the prototype for a whole new genre of fiction: the "sensation no...
commentaries: Susan Sontag references Collins's novel as an example of a work that explores the tension between female beauty and intelligence, specifically describing the character Marian Halcombe.
Northrop Frye cites 'The Woman in White' as an example of a nineteenth-century novel using the convention of two heroines, one dark and one light.

book:877693.description: Don Juan Tenorio, el drama romantico por excelencia, es una de las pocas obras que han tenido y siguen teniendo una vida autenticamente popular. Dificil seria encontrar un espanol que no sepa recitar de memoria alguno de sus versos. El drama, que repite el viejo tema de Don Juan, ha adquirido una eficacia literaria inusitada en la mezcla de temas de capa y espada con los religiosos y morales. Esta edicion se basa en la francesa que Zorrilla dio como definitiva cotejada con el manuscrito autografo conservado...
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges references Zorrilla's play as another example of the Don Juan literary tradition.

book:web_ebeec15b.description: A classic science fiction fix-up novel by Ray Bradbury, depicting the colonization of Mars by humans fleeing a troubled Earth. It is composed of interconnected short stories.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges lists this as a work by Ray Bradbury that he provided a prologue for.

book:13451770.description:
Guy Montag is a fireman. His job is to burn books, which are forbidden, being the source of all discord and unhappiness. Even so, Montag is unhappy; there is discord in his marriage. Are books hidden in his house? The Mechanical Hound of the Fire Department, armed with a lethal hypodermic, escorted by helicopters, is ready to track down those dissidents who defy society to preserve and read books.
The classic novel of a post-literate future, 'Fahrenheit 451' stands alongside Orwell's '1984' and Huxley's 'Br...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Bradbury’s novel as a modern allegory of censorship and the destruction of knowledge through fire.
Umberto Eco cites Bradbury’s novel as a cultural reference point for themes of censorship, fire, and knowledge suppression.

book:web_43030461.description: A collection of poems by Stefan George, considered a central work of the George Circle and German Symbolist literature.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges quotes a line from Stefan George's book 'Der Stern des Bundes' to show a similar expression of identity and duality.

book:web_002028e2.description: A novel by Theodore Dreiser about a young woman from a poor family who becomes involved with wealthy men in late 19th century America.
commentaries: Susan Sontag cites Dreiser's novel 'Jennie Gerhardt' to establish a temporal context for the photographs, aligning their aesthetic with the era of its writing.

book:1323880.description: Theodore Dreiser had a hardscrabble youth and the years of newspaper work behind him when he began his first novel, Sister Carrie, the story of a beautiful Midwestern girl who makes it big in New York City. Published by Doubleday in 1900, it gained a reputation as a shocker, for Dreiser had dared to give the public a heroine whose "cosmopolitan standard of virtue" brings her from Wisconsin, with four dollars in her purse, to a suite at the Waldorf and glittering fame as an actress. With Sister Carrie, the o...
commentaries: Susan Sontag cites Dreiser's novel 'Sister Carrie' to further anchor the photographs in a late 19th-century American literary context, noting its scandalous reception.
Jorge Luis Borges references Ouspensky's book 'Tertium Organum' for its ideas on pre-existent future.

book:web_9ef7d3d1.description: A philosophical allegory and tale of autodidacticism, depicting the spiritual and intellectual development of a solitary man on a desert island. The title translates literally as 'Alive, son of Awake'. It influenced medieval and early modern European thought.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges cites Ibn Tufail's 'Alive, Son of Awake' as a revision of Avicenna's work and a favorite of Ramón Llull.

book:web_df9294af.description: A series of nine homilies by Saint Ambrose of Milan on the six days of Creation, based on the Hexameron of Basil of Caesarea.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges cites St. Ambrose's 'Hexameron' as a source for an example of suicide in nature within Donne's catalog.

book:web_4ec7e24c.description: A psychological study of dreams by the English physician and writer Havelock Ellis, originally published as part of his series 'Studies in the Psychology of Sex' and later issued as a standalone work.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges references Ellis's psychological study to compare Coleridge's dream with another case of dream inspiration.

book:web_aeac75fb.description: A collection of essays on science, society, and politics by the British zoologist and popular science writer Lancelot Hogben.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges mentions Hogben's book as one of the works consulted while writing about John Wilkins.

book:11093132.description: These classic fairy tales have left an indelible mark on Western culture, a testament to the brilliance and skill of Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges notes Chesterton's high regard for this book, linking it to his gothic sensibilities.
Joseph Campbell cites a specific tale from this collection of folklore.

book:web_a7a20098.description: A scholarly work on Germanic runes by one of the Brothers Grimm, published in 1821.

book:web_91110a79.description: Main philosophical work of Philipp Mainländer, presenting a pessimistic philosophy centered on the concept of redemption through the negation of the will to live.

book:web_61847250.description: An influential essay by Spanish philosopher José Ortega y Gasset on the challenges and paradoxes of translation, originally published in Volume V of his Obras completas by Revista de Occidente in 1947.

book:web_4ab46829.description: The Ecclesiastical History of the English People, a Latin work by the Venerable Bede detailing the history of the Christian Church in England from the Roman occupation to 731 AD.

book:15799592.description: Forster's renowned guide to writing sparkles with wit and insight for contemporary writers and readers. He not only defines and explains such terms as "round" characters versus "flat" characters (and why both are needed for an effective novel), but also provides examples of writing from such literary greats as Dickens and Austen. Forst...
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges cites Forster's book to present a critical interpretation of 'Moby-Dick's' spiritual theme.
Northrop Frye references Forster's book to discuss a contrast in narrative repetition.

book:6603748.description: When Adela Quested and her elderly companion Mrs Moore arrive in the Indian town of Chandrapore, they quickly feel trapped by its insular and prejudiced 'Anglo-Indian' community. commentaries: David Foster Wallace quotes Forster to illustrate how language conveys social subtext, using the passage as an epigraph to highlight the gap between literal meaning and social intention.

commentaries: Harold Bloom references the characters Margaret and Helen from Forster's novel Howard's End as part of a tradition of heroines.

book:145108.description: This important work, first published in 1934, is a concise statement of Pound's aesthetic theory. With characteristic vigor and iconoclasm, Pound illustrates his precepts with exhibits meticulously chosen from the classics, and the concluding "Treatise on Meter" provides an illuminating essay for anyone aspiring to read and write poetry. book:269589.description:
Delmore Schwartz said about The Cantos, "They are one of the touchstones of modern poetry." William Carlos Williams said, "[Pound] discloses history by its odor, by the feel of it--in the words; fuses it with the words, present and past, to MAKE his Cantos. Makethem."

commentaries: Northrop Frye mentions Pound's 'Cantos' as an example of the paradoxical technique of encyclopaedic yet discontinuous poetry in the ironic mode.

book:269735.description: Ostensibly a biography of the gaucho barbarian Juan Facundo Quiroga, Facundois also a complex, passionate work of history, sociology, and political commentary, and Latin America's most important essay of the nineteenth century.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges mentions Sarmiento's book Facundo and Borges's opinion on its historical significance.

book:1240002.description: With the clarity that James deemed obligatory, Some Problems of Philosophyoutlines his theory of perception. The early chapters expose the defects of intellectualism and monism and the advantages of empiricism and pluralism. The novelty that enters into concrete perceptual experience, and that is disallowed by the rationalizing intellect, suggests exciting possibilities. Denied any absolute truth in an ever-changing world, privy to only a piece of the truth at any given moment, the individual can, with fait...
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges cites William James's 'Some Problems of Philosophy' for its use of infinite regression to challenge the passage of time.
Jorge Luis Borges states he is following the exposition from James's book.

book:1322540.description:
Being the Gifford Lectures on Natural Religion Delivered in Edinburgh 1901/2
"I am neither a theologian, nor a scholar learned in the history of religions, nor an anthropologist. Psychology is the only branch of learning in which I am particularly versed. book:web_817c142f.description: A satirical fairy tale/romance by Antoine Hamilton, part of his collection of stories. It parodies the conventions of Oriental tales popular in early 18th-century France.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges mentions Hamilton's 'Quatre Facardins' as an influence on Beckford, per Chapman's notes.

book:7520474.description: Through his highly idiosyncratic readings of some of the finest paintings, sculptures, and poems of the French and Italian Renaissance, Walter Pater in Studies in the History of the Renaissanceredefined the practice of criticism as an impressionistic, almost erotic exploration of the critic's aesthetic responses. Pater's infamous "Conclusion," which forever linked him with the decadent movement, scandalized many with its insistence on making pleasure the sole motive of life, even as it charmed fellow aesthe...
commentaries: Umberto Eco identifies Pater's The Renaissance as the origin of the concept of epiphany, linking it to fleeting aesthetic experiences and the metaphor of fire.

book:1216209.description:
Heimskringla(Icelandic pronunciation: ['heims,khriNGla]) is the best known of the Old Norse kings' sagas. It was written in Old Norse in Iceland by the poet and historian Snorri Sturluson (1178/79-1241) ca. 1230. The name Heimskringla was first used in the 17th century, derived from the first two words of one of the manuscripts (kringla heimsins - the circle of the world).
Heimskringla is a collection of sagas about the Norwegian kings, beginning with the saga of the legendary Swedish dynasty of the Yngling...
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges cites Snorri Sturlason's 'Heimskringla' as the historical source for the account of King Harald Sigurdarson's death in battle.

book:24658.description:
'What was the beginning, or how did things start? What was there before?'
The Prose Eddais the most renowned of all works of Scandinavian literature and our most extensive source for Norse mythology. Written in Iceland a century after the close of the Viking Age, it tells ancient stories of the Norse creation epic and recounts the battles that follow as gods, giants, dwarves and elves struggle for survival. It also preserves the oral memory of heroes, warrior kings and queens. In clear prose interspersed wi...
commentaries: Northrop Frye classifies the Prose Edda as a sacred book belonging to the same quintessential form as the Bible, and notes its influence on Finnegans Wake.
Joseph Campbell references a specific translation of the Prose Edda by this translator.

book:web_5e23fcc6.description: A foundational work of Creationist poetry by Chilean poet Vicente Huidobro, published in 1916. The collection represents Huidobro's avant-garde literary movement that emphasized the poet as a creator of new realities rather than an imitator of nature.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges cites Huidobro's book as the source of a poetic image comparing mirrors to water.

book:32724496.description: "Piranesi fu uno dei pochi geni tragici d'Italia, avendo a soli compagni Dante e Michelangelo. E ciascuno di questi geni era tragico, perche con lui si chiudeva un'epoca, un ciclo. Con Dante il Medioevo e secoli di violenza, di amor cortese e di visioni mistiche erano giudicati e riassunti in una costruzione apocalittica. Con Michelangelo il Rinascimento, e un mondo di esaltati titani vacillava sull'orlo della stanchezza, e la volutta di Leda si mutava nel languore tenebroso della Notte. Ma con Piranesi tut...
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges adds Piranesi's 'Carceri d'invenzione' to the list of influences, describing its etchings of labyrinthine palaces as admired by Beckford.

book:1534353.description: A landmark of twentieth-century criticism that provided new standards and new techniques for examining literature. "Richards is a master of the psychology of criticism" (Saturday Review). Index.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges references Richards's book as a comparative point for Borges's critical method, noting a shared starting point but different conclusions.

book:22068883.description: When a young graduate returns home he is accompanied, much to his father and uncle's discomfort, by a strange friend "who doesn't acknowledge any authorities, who doesn't accept a single principle on faith." Turgenev's masterpiece of generational conflict shocked Russian society when it was published in 1862 and continues today to seem as fresh and outspoken as it did to those who first encountered its nihilistic hero.
commentaries: David Foster Wallace quotes Turgenev’s Fathers and Sons to illustrate a radical ideological stance, using it as a literary counterpoint to Dostoevsky’s themes.

David Foster Wallace references Turgenev’s Fathers and Sons as the source of the term 'Nihilists' and as a cultural touchstone for Dostoevsky’s ideological opposition to radical 19th-century Russian youth movements.

book:web_1aa66042.description: A treatise by the French bishop and theologian Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet, criticizing the theater and comedy from a moral and religious perspective. It was written in 1694 as part of his broader campaign against what he perceived as the immoral influence of the stage.
commentaries: Erich Auerbach quotes Bossuet's book to illustrate the theological condemnation of the theater's anti-Christian tendencies in the era.

book:web_40dcffc7.description: A scholarly work on ancient Egyptian religion by the French Egyptologist Jacques Vandier, published in 1949.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges directly quotes Vandier's book to support the point about the magical power of knowing a god's name in ancient Egyptian belief.

book:859694.description: Beckford's Gothic novel, Vathek, an Arabian tale, was originally written in French when the author was 21. It is the story of Caliph Vathek, whose eye can kill at a glance, who makes a pact with the Devil, Eblis.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges references Vathek, the protagonist of William Beckford's Gothic novel, as an example of a romantic hero who emphasizes his differences.
Jorge Luis Borges notes that Beckford's biographer neglects to analyze 'Vathek,' the novel that secured Beckford's fame.
Jorge Luis Borges cites Beckford's 'Vathek' as an example of a work that describes palaces for the five senses, comparing it to Marino's 'Adone'.

book:web_34e9c323.description: A poem by William Blake, part of his prophetic and symbolic works, exploring cyclical themes of human life, creation, and destruction.
commentaries: Northrop Frye references Blake's poem as an example of a vision of the cyclical nature of human life.
Northrop Frye references The Book of Thel as an example of a 'prison-Paradise or unborn world' from which characters seek escape.

Joseph Campbell cites a specific section from Blake's illuminated book.

book:845332.description: The Martin Fierro, the classic argentine poem, has been the subject of studies and discussions ever since the issuing of its first part edition -el gaucho Martin Fierro- in 1873, and there have been many ensuing editions, including some still available, to prove it. This edition is based on the original texts: El gaucho Martin Fierro Imprenta de La Pampa, 1872, and La vuelta de Martin Fierro Libreria del....

Jorge Luis Borges references the epic poem as a comparative example of a narrative structure that returns to its beginning, similar to the plot resolution in the film Morocco.

book:web_949844a9.description: Key work on Argentine Spanish by linguist Arturo Costa Alvarez, published in La Plata in 1928.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges cites Alvarez's work as a key reference on Argentine Spanish, noting its publication year and place.

book:web_dfe1b469.description: Also known as the 'Helmeted Prologue,' this preface by St. Jerome to his Latin Vulgate translation of the Bible discusses the canon of the Hebrew Scriptures, listing the 24 books of the Old Testament according to Jewish tradition.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges cites St. Jerome's 'Prologus Galeatus' as the source for the identification of the twenty-four elders with the books of the Old Testament.

book:web_a56a0633.description: A collection of essays on Spanish literature by the Mexican writer and diplomat Alfonso Reyes.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges quotes from Reyes's book to support an observation about Quevedo's political works, citing a specific page.

book:web_5325ab73.description: A German-language collection and commentary on the pre-Socratic philosophers, edited and translated by Wilhelm Capelle. The work compiles fragments and testimonia of early Greek philosophers.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges references Capelle's book as a source for the translation of Zeno's paradox from Aristotle, noting its publication details.

book:web_0f1ab69b.description: A collection of fantastic tales by German author Kurd Lasswitz, containing the story 'The Universal Library' which imagines a library containing all possible book combinations.

book:11313522.description: Kurd Lasswitz's 1897 utopian novel describes man's first encounter with beings of higher intelligence from another planet, the inhabitants of Mars. Physically differing little from man, but intellectually, ethically, scientifically, and socially far advanced, the Martians seek to educate man, whom they encounter at the North Pole, where they seek air and energy to supplement the diminished supplies in their own, older world. book:9716844.description: Many of the earliest books, particularly those dating back to the 1900s and before, are now extremely scarce and increasingly expensive. We are republishing these classic works in affordable, high quality, modern editions, using the original text and artwork.
commentaries: Northrop Frye quotes Shelley's 'A Defence of Poetry' to illustrate the idea of critics and poets building a collective work across ages.

book:web_56cde088.description: Unfinished visionary poem by Percy Bysshe Shelley, written shortly before his death in 1822 and published posthumously in 1824. The poem is heavily influenced by Dante's works and explores themes of life, death, and human suffering through a dream-vision framework.

book:web_3850853e.description: A famous Persian philosophical and mystical work whose title translates to 'Confluence of the Two Seas' or 'Meeting of the Two Oceans'. book:674355.description:
One of the great masterpieces of Western religious thought, the Zohar represents an attempt to uncover hidden meanings behind the world of appearances. It is the central work in the literature of the Kabbalah, the Jewish mystical tradition.

book:1010394.description: This essential introduction to the poems of Giacomo Leopardi provides a complete translation of The Canti, explanatory notes, and a selection of Leopardi's prose keyed to related poems. Further background is provided by an introduction and a brief biography woven from Leopardi's own words.
commentaries: Umberto Eco quotes Leopardi’s poem as an example of lyrical expression, citing its inclusion in a collected edition.

book:18623541.description: First published in 1915, Ford Madox Ford's The Good Soldierbegins, famously and ominously, "This is the saddest story I have ever heard." The book then proceeds to confute this pronouncement at every turn, exposing a world less sad than pathetic, and more shot through with hypocrisy and deceit than its incredulous narrator, John Dowell, cares to imagine. Somewhat forgotten as a classic, The Good Soldierhas been called everything from the consummate novelist's novel to one of the greatest English works of th...
commentaries: Susan Sontag identifies this novel as a partial inspiration for Glenway Wescott's 'The Pilgrim Hawk', noting its similar tones of tormented diffidence and muffled anguish.
Susan Sontag cites the opening line of the novel as an example of a first-person narration that establishes a tone of sadness and subjective storytelling.

book:12397712.description: Banned in the Soviet Union until 1988, Doctor Zhivago is the epic story of the life and loves of a poet-physician during the turmoil of the Russian Revolution. Taking his family from Moscow to what he hopes will be shelter in the Ural Mountains, Yuri Zhivago finds himself instead embroiled in the battle between the Whites and the Reds, and in love with the tender and beautiful nurse Lara.
commentaries: Sontag references Pasternak's own evaluation of his prose works, including his novel Doctor Zhivago.

book:12424.description: The awarding of the 1958 Nobel Prize for Literature to Boris Pasternak and the subsequent calumny of his fellow citizens in Soviet Russia focused unusual attention on Pasternak's great novel, Dr. Zhivago, and the small body of his other work. At the time, the latter was only available (in any language, as far as is known) in New Directions' Selected Writingsof Pasternak, first published in 1949. The 1958 edition was issued with a new introduction by Babette Deutsch under the title of the book's main compone...
commentaries: Susan Sontag cites this book as one of several that Elizabeth Hardwick found emboldening when writing 'Sleepless Nights'.

book:458275.description: This powerful short novel describes the events of a single afternoon. Alwyn Towers, an American expatriate and sometime novelist, is staying with a friend outside of Paris, when a well-heeled, itinerant Irish couple drops in--with Lucy, their trained hawk, a restless, sullen, disturbingly totemic presence. Lunch is prepared, drink flows. A masquerade, at once harrowing and farcical, begins. A work of classical elegance and concision, The Pilgrim Hawkstands with Faulkner's The Bearas one of the finest Americ...
commentaries: Susan Sontag identifies and praises the novel as a neglected treasure of twentieth-century American literature.
Susan Sontag references the novel's opening as an example of a first-person narrative that evokes temporal distance and reflection on the past.
Susan Sontag references this novel as an example of a work with aphoristic glitter that condenses and distills.
Susan Sontag uses the novel's ending as an example of how biographical facts can inform a fictional narrative.

book:794687.description: Glenway Wescott's poignant story of nineteenth-century Wisconsin was first published in 1927 as the winner of the prestigious Harper Prize. Like F. Scott Fitzgerald and Ernest Hemingway, Wescott left the Midwest behind to live as a writer in 1920s Paris. In this novel, based on Wescott's own life and family, the young Alwyn Tower leaves Wisconsin to travel in Europe, but finds himself haunted by a family of long-dead spirits--his grandparents and great-uncles and aunts, a generation whose young adulthood wa...
commentaries: Susan Sontag references this earlier novel by Wescott to provide biographical context for a character in 'The Pilgrim Hawk'.

book:1304282.description: "There is nothing unusual about the foot, except that it is seven meters high." Nineteen people are dragging, by means of a cable, an immense carcass through the countryside. The carcass is that of the Dead Father, a half-dead, half-alive, part-mechanical, wise, vain, powerful being who still has hopes for himself, although he is, effectively, dead. Thomas, Julie, Edmund, Emma, and the others variously insult, placate, cater to, and defend the Dead Father as the procession moves through the country of the W...
commentaries: Susan Sontag references this novel as an example of a work that goes after the deadpan, mock smoothness of an allegory or fable.
David Foster Wallace identifies Barthelme’s 'The Balloon' as the pivotal story that inspired him to become a writer.

book:web_e58d410b.description: A collection of short stories by Danilo Kiš, originally published in Serbo-Croatian as 'Rani jadi' in 1969. The stories are semi-autobiographical, depicting the childhood of a young boy named Andreas Sam in pre-World War II Yugoslavia.
commentaries: Susan Sontag notes this as the third published book by Danilo Kiš, a collection of stories.

book:1418542.description: Naipaul's controversial account of his travels through the Islamic world was hailed by The New Republic as "the most notable work on contemporary Islam to have appeared in a very long time."
commentaries: Susan Sontag references this book as an example of a travel narrative where a lone observer uses a native cicerone as a principal interlocutor.

book:815322.description: The story of a writer's singular journey--from one place to another, from the British colony of Trinidad to the ancient countryside of England, and from one state of mind to another--this is perhaps Naipaul's most autobiographical work. Yet it is also woven through with remarkable invention to make it a rich and complex novel.
commentaries: Susan Sontag references the novel as an instance where the narrator's identity closely aligns with Susan Sontag's own, questioning the boundaries of the novel form.
Susan Sontag cites this novel as another example of spiritual autobiography that excludes the narrator's spouse.
Susan Sontag mentions directing a play by Pirandello as a prior experience of working in a foreign language.

book:151447.description: Not so long ago Emilio Brentani was a promising young author. Now he is an insurance agent on the fast track to forty. He gains a new lease on life, though, when he falls for the young and gorgeous Angiolina-except that his angel just happens to be an unapologetic cheat. But what begins as a comedy of infatuated misunderstanding ends in tragedy, as Emilio's jealous persistence in his folly-against his friends' and devoted sister's advice, and even his own best knowledge-leads to the loss of the one person w...
commentaries: Susan Sontag cites this work alongside 'Confessions of Zeno' as belonging to a specific narrative tradition.

book:web_2e10d414.description: A modernist novel written in the form of a psychoanalyst's case study of Zeno Cosini, exploring themes of self-deception, addiction, and the human condition.
commentaries: Susan Sontag cites these works by Svevo as part of the same narrative tradition stemming from Sterne.

Susan Sontag references Gottfried von Strassburg's epic as the most comprehensive source for the Celtic legend of Tristan and Isolde, specifically detailing the origin and accidental consumption of the love potion.

book:18746840.description:
'We believe in her as in a woman we might providentially meet some fine day when we should find ourselves doubting of the immortality of the soul'
wrote Henry James of Dorothea Brooke, who shares with the young doctor Tertius Lydgate not only a central role in Middlemarchbut also a fervent conviction that life should be heroic.
By the time the novel appeared to tremendous popular and critical acclaim in 1871-2, George Eliot was recognized as England's finest living novelist. It was her ambition to create a....
commentaries: Susan Sontag mentions this novel as an example of a work that employs essayistic digressions to pursue completeness.
Harold Bloom references George Eliot's novel 'Middlemarch' to discuss the concept of 'commonness' in characters.

book:web_194d11c4.description: Photography book documenting rural white South Africans during apartheid's final years
commentaries: Susan Sontag references Roger Ballen's book 'Platteland' as a comparative example of photographic work depicting subjects considered unattractive, contrasting its political message with the work under discussion.

book:web_dbf81389.description: Play by the Croatian writer Miroslav Krleža, originally published in 1928. The title translates to 'In Agony' or 'In Agonie' in English. It is one of Krleža's early dramatic works exploring social and psychological themes.
commentaries: Susan Sontag references Krleža's play 'In Agony' as one of the productions in Sarajevo, noting its thematic relevance.

book:8585068.description: Widely regarded as the father of modern Western philosophy, Descartes sought to look beyond established ideas and create a thought system based on reason. In this profound work he meditates on doubt, the human soul, God, truth and the nature of existence itself.
commentaries: Susan Sontag references Descartes's 'Meditations' as a philosophical work that influenced her approach to her first novel.
David Foster Wallace references Descartes’ Meditations as a foundational philosophical text that influenced his perspective.

book:8058415.description: Rene Descartes is perhaps most remembered for declaring, I think; therefore, I am. First published in 1644, Descartes s "Principles of Philosophy" elucidates the meaning of those words that ushered in a new era of philosophical thought. Unlike the medieval philosophers who often began by examining the existence and nature of God in a spirit of faith, Descartes begins by reflecting upon himself as one who doubts but who nonetheless desires certain knowledge of God and the world. In setting forth the truths h...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Descartes’ work to illustrate a compromise hypothesis that reconciled heliocentrism with church doctrine through the mechanism of celestial vortexes.

book:11124891.description: Descartes' Discourse marks a watershed in European thought; in it, the author sets out in brief his radical new philosophy, which begins with a proof of the existence of the self (the famous "cogito ergo sum"). Next he deduces from it the existence and nature of God, and ends by offering a radical new account of the physical world and of human and animal nature. Written in everyday language and meant to be read by common people of the day, it swept away all previous philosophical traditions
commentaries: David Foster Wallace references Descartes’ Discourse on Method alongside the Meditations as a key philosophical work.
Susan Sontag specifies reading Halliburton's book 'Book of Marvels' in 1940, describing it as a prime awakener of her own ardor and appetite for the world.

book:300818.description: Is there any such thing as revolutionary literature? Can literature, in fact, be political at all? These are the questions Roland Barthes addresses in Writing Degree Zero, his first published book and a landmark in his oeuvre. The debate had engaged the European literary community since the 1930s; with this fierce manifesto, Barthes challenged the notion of literature's obligation to be socially committed. Yes, Barthes allows, the writer has a political and ethical responsibility. But the history of French....
commentaries: Susan Sontag quotes directly from Barthes's first book to illustrate his view on literature's brilliance at the moment it attempts to die.

book:765227.description: What is it that we do when we enjoy a text? What is the pleasure of reading? The French critic and theorist Roland Barthes's answers to these questions constitute "perhaps for the first time in the history of criticism . . . not only a poetics of reading . . . but a much more difficult achievement, an erotics of reading . . . . Like filings which gather to form a figure in a magnetic field, the parts and pieces here do come together, determined to affirm the pleasure we must take in our reading as against t...
commentaries: Susan Sontag cites Barthes's book as an example of his inventive classifications used to structure an argument.

book:7754.description: In Waiting for Godot, two wandering tramps, Vladimir and Estragon, wait by a lonely tree, to meet up with Mr. Godot, an enigmatic figure in a world where time, place and memory are blurred and meaning is where you find it. The tramps hope that Godot will change their lives for the better. Instead, two eccentric travelers arrive, one man on the end of the other's rope. The results are both funny and dangerous in this existential masterpiece.
commentaries: Susan Sontag references the opening line of Beckett's play to set the context for the narrative.
Susan Sontag notes that the Sarajevo audience expects plays such as 'Waiting for Godot', indicating its status as a significant European work relevant to their cultural identity.
Susan Sontag mentions being focused on directing Samuel Beckett's play 'Waiting for Godot' in Sarajevo.
Susan Sontag references the play 'Waiting for Godot' being performed in Sarajevo, indicating its cultural significance in the wartime context.
Susan Sontag mentions bringing copies of the play for a production in Sarajevo.
Susan Sontag notes that this Beckett play was well-known and frequently performed in the former Yugoslavia.

book:214598.description:
As one enters Juan Rulfo's legendary novel, one follows a dusty road to a town of death. Time shifts from one consciousness to another in a hypnotic flow of dreams, desires, and memories, a world of ghosts dominated by the figure of Pedro Paramo - lover, overlord, murderer.
Rulfo's extraordinary mix of sensory images, violent passions and unfathomable mysteries has been a profound influence on a whole generation of Latin American writers including Carlos Fuentes, Mario Vargas Llosa and Gabriel Garcia Marque...
commentaries: Susan Sontag analyzes Rulfo's novel, praising its narrative structure, concision, and its status as a legendary work in Mexican literature.
Susan Sontag cites García Márquez's deep admiration for the book, noting it was a foundational text he memorized.

book:3243919.description:
Libro de relatos perfectos, profundamente enraizados en un momento historico muy concreto, los anos cincuenta, cuando ya era evidente el fracaso de la Revolucion mexicana y apuntaban los comienzos del 'desarrollo' mas salvaje. La obra de Rulfo, sin embargo, va mucho mas alla de la excelente literatura mexicana que se ocupa de los mismos temas - como Los de abajo, de Mariano Azuela - y junto con su novela Pedro Paramo, marca un momento limite de las letras hispanoamericanas.
Tras la publicacion de los dos li...
commentaries: Susan Sontag mentions Rulfo's story collection, noting its English translation title and its role in establishing his literary reputation.
Northrop Frye cites Pope's work as an example of how a word can have multiple meanings within a poetic context, contrasting this with assertive writing where such ambiguity would cause confusion.
Northrop Frye notes that Pope describes and exemplifies the device of imitative harmony in his work 'Essay on Criticism'.
Harold Bloom cites this work as an instance where Pope connects extrinsic embellishments to a known subject, illustrating his invention.

book:10139547.description: The 18th century was a wealth of knowledge, exploration and rapidly growing technology and expanding record-keeping made possible by advances in the printing press. In its determination to preserve the century of revolution, Gale initiated a revolution of its own: digitization of epic proportions to preserve these invaluable works in the largest archive of its kind. Now for the first time these high-quality digital copies of original 18th century manuscripts are available in print, making them highly access...
commentaries: Harold Bloom mentions this poem as an example where Pope's imagination conveys energies of passion.

book:21362296.description: WHAT dire Offence from am'rous Causes springs, What mighty Contests rise from trivial Things, I sing -- This Verse to C---, Muse is due; This, ev'n Belinda may vouchfafe to view: Slight is the Subject, but not so the Praise, If She inspire, and He approve my Lays.
commentaries: Harold Bloom references this poem as an example of Pope's inventive genius, according to Johnson's analysis.

book:web_39e6c2a0.description: A collection of four moral essays in verse by Alexander Pope, also known as the 'Ethick Epistles' or 'Moral Essays', addressing topics like the characters of men and women, the use of riches, and the nature of happiness.
commentaries: Harold Bloom cites these epistles as works where Pope's imagination impresses forms of nature and life.

book:web_cd5a428e.description: A topographical poem by Alexander Pope celebrating the peace following the Treaty of Utrecht, blending pastoral description with political commentary.
commentaries: Harold Bloom references this poem as another demonstration of Pope's imaginative power in depicting nature.

book:5613536.description: This work has been selected by scholars as being culturally important, and is part of the knowledge base of civilization as we know it. This work was reproduced from the original artifact, and remains as true to the original work as possible. Therefore, you will see the original copyright references, library stamps (as most of these works have been housed in our most important libraries around the world), and other notations in the work.This work is in the public domain in the United States of America, and....
commentaries: Harold Bloom describes Johnson's critical dismissal of this philosophical poem by Pope.
Harold Bloom notes Johnson's high regard for this work by Pope, considering it superior to the Essay on Man.

book:web_f57010c5.description: Simone de Beauvoir's travelogue about her trip to China in 1955, first published in French as 'La Chine au jour le jour' in 1958.
commentaries: Susan Sontag cites this book as an example of the common form of travel writing about revolutionary countries, describing it as a notably ingenuous account of a trip.

book:7191.description:
The Man in the Iron Maskis the final episode in the cycle of novels featuring Dumas celebrated foursome of D Artagnan, Athos, Porthos and Aramis, who first appeared in The Three Musketeers.
Some thirty-five years on, the bonds of comradeship are under strain as they end up on different sides in a power struggle that may undermine the young Louis XIV and change the face of the French monarchy.
In the fast-paced narrative style that was his trademark, Dumas pitches us straight into the action. What is the sec...
commentaries: Susan Sontag uses the novel as a simile to describe the feeling of being trapped behind one's own face while being photographed.

book:3646333.description:
Alexandre Dumas
Alexandre Dumas lahir di Villers-Cotterets, Perancis, tanggal 24 Juli 1802. Kakeknya soerang bangsawan, neneknya wanita berkulit hitam dari Santo Domingo. Ayahnya seorang jenderal balatentara Napoleon, yang gugur pada saat Dumas baru berumur empat tahun, tanpa meninggalkan kekayaan sedikit pun. Ia dipelihara oleh seorang pendeta, kemudian bekerja sebagai juru tulis kantor pengacara. Pada saat usia dua puluh satu tahun ia pindah ke Paris, mengabdi pada seorang bangsawan. Perkenalannya dengan....
commentaries: Umberto Eco repeatedly cites Monte-Cristo as a case study in how a linguistically flawed novel can achieve literary status through narrative archetypes and structural wisdom.
Umberto Eco reiterates Monte-Cristo as an exemplar of a 'sludgy simple form'—a long novel that achieves mythic power despite stylistic shortcomings.
Umberto Eco analyzes Monte-Cristo as a narrative deeply structured by Christological archetypes, elevating it beyond its stylistic flaws through mythic resonance.
Umberto Eco cites Dumas’s memoir to highlight the enduring reality of fictional characters compared to historical figures, emphasizing the power of literary creation.
Umberto Eco cites Dumas’s The Count of Monte Cristo as an example of how excess and stylistic flaws, when amplified, can produce a Kantian sublime effect in literature.

book:742106.description:
One of the most celebrated & popular historical romances ever written. The Three Musketeers tell the story of the early adventures of the young Gascon gentleman d'Artagnan & his three friends from the regiment of the King's Musketeers-Athos, Porthos & Aramis.
Under the watchful eye of their patron M. de Treville, the four defend the honour of the regiment against the guards of the Cardinal Richelieu, & the honor of the queen against the machinations of the Cardinal himself as the power struggles of 17th-cen...
commentaries: Umberto Eco contrasts The Three Musketeers with Monte-Cristo, praising it as a well-crafted example of narrative energy, despite Dumas’s commercial motivations.
Umberto Eco references The Three Musketeers as a contrasting example of Dumas’s superior craftsmanship, used to highlight the deliberate excess in The Count of Monte Cristo.
Umberto Eco cites Dumas’s The Three Musketeers as the authoritative textual source for the character D’Artagnan, contrasting popular perception with the original narrative detail.

book:12838589.description:
This book was lost for centuries to the western world, although it was kept by the Ethiopian church. In 1773, the Scottish explorer James Bruce heard that the Book of Enoch may have been in Ethiopia, so he traveled there and procured three copies. In 1821, Richard Laurence, a professor of Hebrew at Oxford, produced the first English translation. Fragments of ten Enoch manuscripts were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls. It is quoted by the New Testament Book of Jude.
This book contains all sections:
The Book....
commentaries: Susan Sontag cites Wycliffe's translation of the Book of Enoch to illustrate the etymological and spiritual concept of translation as a transfer from death to life.

book:1555826.description: In this historic romance, young Elizabeth Bennet strives for love, independence and honesty in the vapid high society of 19th century England.
commentaries: Susan Sontag quotes and analyzes the famous opening line, attributing it sarcastically to Jane Austen and discussing its role as a generalization at the beginning of a novel.
Northrop Frye uses Austen's novel as an example to discuss how a shift in focus could undermine humor and evoke a sense of nightmare in comedy.
Northrop Frye contrasts Austen's Pride and Prejudice with Hyperion as examples of the division between fictional and thematic works in the low mimetic mode.
Harold Bloom quotes Woolf speculating about Austen's circumstances affecting her writing.

book:15828826.description: Sens and Sensibility's two heroines - so utterly unlike each other - undergo the most violent passions when they are separated from the men they love. What differentiates them, and gives this extraordinary book its complexity and brilliance is the way each expresses her suffering. Marianne - young, impetuous, ardent - falls into paroxysms of grief when she is rejected by the dashing John Willoughby; while her sister, Elinor - wiser, more sensible, more self-controlled - masks her despair when it appears tha...
commentaries: Northrop Frye cites Austen's novel as an example of a work named for its theme, while noting Austen's interest in storytelling.

book:2534657.description: In Northanger Abbey, a young woman's penchant for sensational Gothic novels leads to misunderstandings in the matters of the heart. Austen's first, this is considered by many to be among her most charming novels.
commentaries: Northrop Frye lists this novel as an example of a work that parodies romance conventions.

book:23247049.description: Laurence Sterne's great masterpiece of bawdy humour and rich satire defies any attempt to categorize it. Part novel, part digression, its gloriously disordered narrative interweaves the birth and life of the unfortunate "hero" Tristram Shandy, the eccentric philosophy of his father Walter, the amours and military obsessions of Uncle Toby, and a host of other characters, including Dr. Slop, Corporal Trim and the parson Yorick. A joyful celebration of the endless possibilities of the art of fiction, Tristram....
commentaries: Susan Sontag notes a specific narrative parallel, framing it as an homage by Machado de Assis to Sterne's work.
Susan Sontag asserts the influential authority of Sterne's book on a later Brazilian writer.
Susan Sontag references Nietzsche's admiration for the novel to illustrate its significant influence in world literature.
Susan Sontag states that Sterne's book holds a central place in the theoretical work of Russian formalists like Viktor Shklovsky.
Susan Sontag compares the visual documents in the discussed work to the squiggles in Sterne's novel *Tristram Shandy*, noting a similar authorial intimacy.
Susan Sontag cites this book as the principal model for the narrative procedures of reader awareness discussed in the text.
Harold Bloom mentions Johnson's erroneous judgment that Sterne's Tristram Shandy would not endure.
Susan Sontag references Gombrowicz's novel as a work where the protagonist reflects Susan Sontag's own personality and pathology.
Susan Sontag discusses the novel's enduring relevance and its author's self-mythologizing, noting how its targets have become dated but its brilliance remains.

book:web_ed042838.description: Witold Gombrowicz's debut collection of short stories, published in 1933. The English title is often translated as 'Memoirs of a Time of Immaturity' or 'Diary of a Time of Immaturity.' It was poorly received upon publication, which Gombrowicz later referenced ironically in his works.
commentaries: Susan Sontag cites a fictional book within Gombrowicz's novel, presented as a work by the protagonist, to illustrate Susan Sontag's self-referential narrative strategy.

book:18185.description:
"The Pillow Book of Sei Shonagon" is a fascinating, detailed account of Japanese court life in the eleventh century. Written by a lady of the court at the height of Heian culture, this book enthralls with its lively gossip, witty observations, and subtle impressions.
Lady Shonagon was an erstwhile rival of Lady Murasaki, whose novel, "The Tale of Genji," fictionalized the elite world Lady Shonagon so eloquently relates. Featuring reflections on royal and religious ceremonies, nature, conversation, poetry, a...
commentaries: Susan Sontag cites Sei Shōnagon's Pillow Book as an early formulation of aesthetic standards in Japan, describing it as a breviary of dandy attitudes.

book:890204.description: The ABC book is a Polish genre, a literary form loosely composed of short, alphabetically arranged entries. In this "splendid" volume (Edward Hirsch, The New York Times Book Review), Czeslaw Milosz's telling eye for detail and sharp judgements create unforgettable portraits as he combines sketches of characters from his earlier prose works and poems with references to real historical figures. Simone de Beauvoir, Albert Camus, Fyodor Dostoevsky, Edward Hopper, and Arthur Koestler are among those who come und...
commentaries: Susan Sontag references Milosz's book 'Milosz’s ABC’s' to discuss the presence of history and contrasts it with Gombrowicz's themes.

book:909746.description: "I am a deceased writer not in the sense of one who has written and is now deceased, but in the sense of one who had died and is now writing." So begins the posthumous memoir of Braz Cubas, a wealthy nineteenth-century Brazilian. Though the grave has given Cubas the distance to examine his rather undistinguished life, it has not dampened his sense of humor. In the tradition of Laurence Stern's Tristram Shamdy, Epitaph of a Small Winner is one of the wittiest self-portraits in literary history.
commentaries: Susan Sontag recounts her editor suggesting her work was influenced by Machado de Assis's novel, which she later read and acknowledged.
Susan Sontag expresses personal preference for this novel by Machado de Assis, considering it a masterpiece.

book:3435122.description: Dom Casmurro foi escrito em 1899. Seu personagem principal e Bento Santiago, o narrador da historia que, contada em primeira pessoa, pretende "atar as duas pontas da vida", ou seja, unir relatos desde sua mocidade ate os dias em que esta escrevendo o livro. Entre esses dois momentos Bento escreve sobre suas reminiscencias da juventude, sua vida no seminario, seu caso com Capitu e o ciume que advem desse relacionamento, que se torna o enredo central da trama. Ambientado no Rio de Janeiro do Segundo Imperio,....
commentaries: Susan Sontag notes that critics often favor Machado de Assis's later novel 'Dom Casmurro' over 'Memórias póstumas de Brás Cubas'.

book:18498459.description: 'Der Judenstaat.: Versuch einer modernen Losung der Judenfrage' ist ein Buch von Theodor Herzl, mit dem er versuchte, eine judische Antwort auf die damals so genannte Judenfrage aufzuzeigen. 'Der Judenstaat' ist kein religioses Werk, es hat vielmehr das moderne Judentum massgeblich politisch beeinflusst, indem es das Fundament des politischen Zionismus legte. Fur Herzl war ein Judenstaat einerseits wegen des weltweit vorhandenen Antisemitismus notwendig, andererseits weil die Religion durch die Folgen der A...
commentaries: Susan Sontag cites a sentence from Herzl's book to illustrate how European colonization was justified as extending civilization against barbarism.

book:web_8a5a70c1.description: A prose book by Polish poet and essayist Adam Zagajewski, reflecting on his childhood in industrial Gliwice and the lost beauty of Lwów (Lviv). The English translation was published in 1995.
commentaries: Susan Sontag quotes from Zagajewski's book 'Two Cities' to illustrate his personal history and sense of displacement.
